args.command:
mkdir -p /workspace/specs && cat > /workspace/specs/builtins_vars.md <<'SPEC_EOF'
# nsh 0.4.2 — Spec: variable-related builtins (export, unset, set, shift, exit, return, alias, unalias, local, readonly)

Probed by running `/workspace/executable --norc -c '...'` with isolated HOME.
Unless noted otherwise, stdout is empty. Error messages go to **stderr**.
When a builtin error occurs mid-script, the error is printed, `$?` is set (usually 1),
and **execution continues** with the next command. The exit code of the whole `-c`
run is the exit status of the **last** command executed.

---

## 1. export

### 1.1 `export` with no arguments
    input:  export
    stdout: (empty)
    stderr: (empty)
    exit:   0
Prints NOTHING (no `declare -x` listing, no variable list). Also true when
variables have been exported earlier (`export A=1 B=2; export` still prints nothing).

### 1.2 `export A=1 B=2` (multiple assignments)
    input:  export A=1 B=2; sh -c "echo [$A][$B]"
    stdout: [1][2]
    exit:   0
Multiple `NAME=VALUE` arguments are all processed.

### 1.3 `export A` (mark existing variable)
    input:  A=5; export A; sh -c "echo child=[$A]"
    stdout: child=[5]
    exit:   0

### 1.4 `export NONEXISTENT` (no such variable)
    input:  export NEWVAR; env | grep NEWVAR; echo grep_rc=$?
    stdout: grep_rc= 1
    exit:   0
Silently does nothing; no variable (not even an empty one) is created.

### 1.5 NO name validation — invalid names are silently accepted and exported
    input:  export 1BAD=2; env | grep 1BAD
    stdout: 1BAD=2
    exit:   0
    input:  export BAD-NAME=3; env | grep BAD
    stdout: BAD-NAME=3
    exit:   0
No error message, exit 0. (Note: `echo "[$1BAD]"` prints `[2]` because `$1` is
positional param 1 (empty) followed by literal text — unrelated to export.)

### 1.6 Flags are silently ignored
    input:  export -n A=1; echo "A=$A"      -> stdout: A=1        (A exported normally)
    input:  export -z A=1; echo "A=$A"      -> stdout: A=1        (unknown flag also ignored)
    input:  export -- A=1; echo "A=$A"      -> stdout: A=1        (-- consumed)
    input:  export -n                      -> no output, exit 0
    input:  export --help                  -> no output, exit 0   (NOT treated as help!)
All exit 0, no output, no error. Any `-x`/`--xxx` token is simply dropped.

### 1.7 **export is effectively a NO-OP: ALL shell variables are visible to children**
    input:  A=5; sh -c "echo noexport=[$A]"
    stdout: noexport=[5]
    exit:   0
A plain (never exported) shell variable appears in a child process's environment.
So `export` has no observable effect at all; every shell variable is passed to
external commands.

### 1.8 unset after export removes it from the environment
    input:  export A=1; unset A; sh -c "echo afterunset=[$A]"; echo "shell=[$A]"
    stdout: afterunset=[]
            shell=[]
    exit:   0

RULES (export):
- exit status always 0.
- never prints anything, never errors.
- parses args: tokens starting with `-` are discarded; `NAME=VALUE` tokens assign
  (any byte string as NAME, no validation); bare `NAME` tokens are no-ops unless
  the variable exists (and even then, no observable difference — see 1.7).
- all shell variables are always passed to child processes' environments.

---

## 2. unset

Uses clap-style argument parsing. Takes EXACTLY ONE argument `<NAME>`.

### 2.1 success
    input:  A=1; unset A; echo "[$A]"
    stdout: []
    exit:   0
Also removes the variable from the environment seen by children (see 1.8).

### 2.2 unset of nonexistent variable
    input:  unset NOPE; echo after
    stdout: after
    exit:   0
No error.

### 2.3 no arguments — clap error (exact stderr, note trailing blank line)
    input:  unset
    stderr:
nsh: unset: error: The following required arguments were not provided:
    <NAME>

USAGE:
    unset <NAME>

For more information try --help

    exit:   1   (message ends with a trailing blank line, i.e. "...--help\n\n")

### 2.4 extra arguments — clap error, NOTHING is unset (atomic)
    input:  A=1 B=2; unset A B; echo "[$A][$B]"
    stdout: [1][2]
    stderr:
nsh: unset: error: Found argument 'B' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

USAGE:
    unset <NAME>

For more information try --help

    exit (of unset): 1;  $? is set to 1; script continues.
    A is NOT unset — the whole command fails before doing anything.

### 2.5 flags -f / -v are rejected
    input:  unset -f foo
    stderr:
nsh: unset: error: Found argument '-f' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

USAGE:
    unset <NAME>

For more information try --help

    exit: 1.  Same shape for `unset -v A` (with '-v' in the message).

### 2.6 accepted oddities
    input:  unset -- A      -> exit 0, unsets A ("--" is consumed by clap)
    input:  unset ""        -> exit 0, no error
    input:  unset A=1       -> exit 0 (treated as a literal name; nothing happens)

### 2.7 `unset --help` — help printed to STDERR, exit 1 (exact text)
nsh: unset: unset 0.4.2
Set command.

USAGE:
    unset <NAME>

FLAGS:
    -h, --help       Prints help information
    -V, --version    Prints version information

ARGS:
    <NAME>    

(Note: description says "Set command." — copy-paste bug; the `<NAME>` line has
4 trailing spaces; output ends with a blank line; stdout stays EMPTY.)

RULES (unset):
- exactly one NAME required; clap errors: message to stderr, `$?`=1, script continues.
- error prefix is `nsh: unset: ` (with the nsh: prefix, unlike shift).
- success (including unknown names, `--`, empty string) => exit 0, silent.
- failure is atomic: on arg-parse error no variable is removed.

---

## 3. set

### 3.1 `set` with no arguments
    input:  A=1 B=hello; set
    stdout: (empty)
    exit:   0
Prints NOTHING — no variable list, no function list.

### 3.2 accepted flags (from clap): only -e, -n, -u, -h/--help, -V/--version
`set --help` exact stderr (stdout EMPTY, exit 1; note trailing spaces on the
bare-flag lines and the trailing blank line):

nsh: set: set 0.4.2
Set command.

USAGE:
    set [FLAGS]

FLAGS:
    -e               
    -h, --help       Prints help information
    -n               
    -u               
    -V, --version    Prints version information


`set -V` / `set --version` (exit 1):
    stdout: "set 0.4.2"     (9 bytes, NO trailing newline)
    stderr: "nsh: set: \n\n"  (literally `nsh: set: ` followed by two newlines)

### 3.3 `set -e` (errexit) — WORKS
    input:  set -e; false; echo SHOULD_NOT_PRINT
    stdout: (empty)
    exit:   1
Shell aborts at the first failing command; exit code is that command's status.
Also aborts on command-not-found:
    input:  set -e; nosuchcmd; echo nope
    stderr: nsh: command not found `nosuchcmd'
    exit:   1
Applies inside function bodies too (aborts the whole shell):
    input:  set -e; f() { false; echo no; }; f; echo after
    stdout: (empty)   exit: 1
`set +e` does NOT exist:
    input:  set +e
    stderr:
nsh: set: error: Found argument '+e' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

USAGE:
    set [FLAGS]

For more information try --help

    ($?=1, script continues; the error does NOT abort the script even under -e
    unless -e was already active... observed: without prior -e, execution continues.)

### 3.4 `set -u` (nounset) — WORKS
    input:  set -u; echo $UNDEFINED_XYZ; echo after
    stderr: nsh: undefined variable `UNDEFINED_XYZ'
    exit:   1
Exact message (with trailing \n):  nsh: undefined variable `NAME'
The expansion error ABORTS the whole script ("after" is not printed) even
without -e.

### 3.5 `set -n` (noexec) — accepted; nothing after it executes
    input:  set -n; echo hi
    stdout: (empty)
    exit:   0
BUT the whole `-c` string is still parsed up front, so later syntax errors
still produce a parse error and exit 255:
    input:  set -n; this is (( garbage
    stderr: nsh: parse error:  --> 1:17
      |
    1 | set -n; this is (( garbage
      |                 ^---
      |
      = expected EOI, word, redirect_direction, heredoc, and_or_list_sep, or compound_list_sep
    exit:   255

### 3.6 combined flags
    input:  set -eu; echo ok     -> stdout: ok, exit 0  (combos accepted)

### 3.7 everything else is a clap error (exit 1, $? =1, script continues)
    input:  set -- a b c
    stderr:
nsh: set: error: Found argument 'a' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

USAGE:
    set [FLAGS]

For more information try --help

    input:  set -x      -> same shape, 'Found argument '-x' ...'
    input:  set -o      -> same shape, 'Found argument '-o' ...'
    input:  set foo     -> same shape, 'Found argument 'foo' ...'

RULES (set):
- There is NO way to set positional parameters: `set -- a b c` is rejected
  ($# stays 0 in `-c` mode; $1.. are only ever function arguments).
- `set` never lists variables or functions.
- only flags: -e, -n, -u (plus clap's -h/--help, -V/--version).
- -e and -u have real semantics; -n stops execution of the rest of the program.
- unknown flags/args: clap error to stderr, status 1, execution continues.
- `--help`/`-h` and `--version`/`-V` go through an error path: help to STDERR
  (stdout empty), exit status 1, and for -V stdout gets `set 0.4.2` with no
  newline while stderr gets `nsh: set: \n\n`.

## 4. shift

clap-based; usage `shift [n]`, optional single numeric arg, default 1.
Note: error messages are prefixed `shift: ` WITHOUT the `nsh: ` prefix
(unlike unset/set), because the shell prints the clap error differently here.

### 4.1 basic operation (inside functions; top-level has no positional params)
    input:  f() { shift; echo "in fn $# $1"; }; f a b c
    stdout: in fn 2 b
    exit:   0
    input:  f() { shift 2; echo "$# [$1]"; }; f a b c
    stdout: 1 [c]
    exit:   0
    input:  f() { shift 0; echo "$# $1"; }; f a b
    stdout: 2 a
    exit:   0

### 4.2 shifting past the end — silent success
    input:  f() { shift 5; echo "n=$#"; }; f a b
    stdout: n=0
    exit:   0
No error; params just become empty. `$?` after shift = 0.

### 4.3 shift with no positional parameters at all
    input:  shift
    stdout: (empty)   stderr: (empty)   exit: 0
    input:  shift 2   -> same, exit 0.

### 4.4 errors (exit status 1, script continues)
    input:  shift abc
    stderr (exact; ends with blank line):
shift: error: Invalid value for '<n>': invalid digit found in string

    input:  shift -1
    stderr:
shift: error: Found argument '-1' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

USAGE:
    shift [n]

For more information try --help

    input:  shift 1 2
    stderr: same shape, 'Found argument '2' ...'

### 4.5 `shift --help` (stderr, exit 1, stdout empty; `<n>` line has 4 trailing spaces)
shift: shift 0.4.2
shift command.

USAGE:
    shift [n]

FLAGS:
    -h, --help       Prints help information
    -V, --version    Prints version information

ARGS:
    <n>    


NOTE: script-level positional params cannot be supplied via the CLI:
`./executable --norc script.sh a b c` fails with
    error: Found argument 'a' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

    USAGE:
        executable --norc

    For more information try --help
(exit 1). So `shift` is only observable inside functions in practice.

## 5. exit

### 5.1 normal numeric argument
    input:  exit 5        -> no output, process exit code 5
    input:  echo before; exit 3; echo after
    stdout: before        exit: 3   (terminates immediately)
    input:  f() { exit 3; }; f; echo no
    (no output)           exit: 3   (exit inside a function exits the shell)

### 5.2 no argument — ALWAYS exits 0 (NOT the last command's status!)
    input:  false; exit   -> exit code 0
    input:  true;  exit   -> exit code 0
    input:  exit          -> exit code 0

### 5.3 argument is parsed as a Rust i32 (decimal, optional sign, NO spaces/junk)
    exit 300      -> 44   (value mod 256 via process exit)
    exit 256      -> 0
    exit 65536    -> 0
    exit -1       -> 255
    exit +5       -> 5    (leading '+' accepted)
    exit 08       -> 8    (leading zeros ok)
    exit abc      -> 1    (parse failure: NO message, exit code 1)
    exit 12abc    -> 1
    exit ""       -> 1
    exit " 7"     -> 1    (leading space not allowed)
    exit 0x10     -> 1
    exit 99999999999999999999 -> 1  (i32 overflow)

### 5.4 extra arguments are silently ignored
    input:  exit 1 2      -> exit code 1, no output

RULES (exit):
- `exit [N]`; missing N => 0; unparseable N => 1 (silently); otherwise N as i32,
  process exit code = N mod 256 (OS truncation of negative/large values).
- extra args ignored; never prints anything.

## 6. return

### 6.1 inside a function: stops the function, status is ALWAYS 0 (argument IGNORED)
    input:  f() { return; echo NO; }; f; echo "after $?"
    stdout: after 0        (function body stops at return)
    input:  f() { return 7; }; f; echo rc=$?
    stdout: rc= 0          (NOT 7! return's numeric argument has no effect)
    input:  f() { false; return; }; f; echo rc=$?
    stdout: rc= 0          (even a preceding failure is discarded)
    input:  f() { return 300; }; f; echo rc=$?
    stdout: rc= 0
    input:  f() { return 7; }; f          (as last command)
    exit:   0
(The space in "rc= 0" is the unquoted-expansion word-splitting quirk — see §10.)

### 6.2 grammar: `return` takes nothing or a single unsigned decimal `num`
    input:  f() { return abc; }; f
    stderr:
nsh: parse error:  --> 1:14
  |
1 | f() { return abc; }; f
  |              ^---
  |
  = expected num, and_or_list_sep, or compound_list_sep
    exit: 255  (whole program rejected at parse time)
    input:  f() { return -1; }; f   -> parse error, same shape ("expected num, ...")
    input:  f() { return 1 2; }; f  -> parse error:
      = expected and_or_list_sep or compound_list_sep   (at the second token)
    `return 08` is accepted (leading zeros fine), status still 0.

### 6.3 OUTSIDE a function: PANIC (top level of -c, script file, or sourced file)
    input:  return            (also: return 5; also `return 3` inside a sourced file)
    stdout: (whatever ran before, e.g. `echo before; return` prints "before")
    stderr (first two lines, deterministic):
nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:133:14:
unexpected Return
    ...then a Rust backtrace (NONDETERMINISTIC addresses; each line prefixed
    with "nsh:    " — the panic hook prefixes all stderr with "nsh: ")...
    ...then a blank line and the final deterministic line:
nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues
    exit: 101
Commands after `return` do not run. (Also writes a log to ~/.nsh.log.)

RULES (return):
- in function: unwinds the function, sets status 0, ignores its argument.
- outside function: process panics with exit 101.

## 7. alias

Custom-parsed (NOT clap). Takes ZERO or ONE argument.

### 7.1 `alias` with no args — list all aliases
    input:  alias
    stdout: (empty)            exit: 0     (when no aliases defined)
    input:  alias ll='ls -l'; alias
    stdout: ll='ls -l'
    exit:   0
Format per line:  NAME='VALUE'\n   (raw value between single quotes, NO escaping)
    input:  alias x="echo 'q u'"; alias
    stdout: x='echo 'q u''
**ORDER IS NONDETERMINISTIC** (Rust HashMap iteration). Two identical runs:
    run1: z='echo z' / m='echo m' / a='echo a'
    run2: m='echo m' / a='echo a' / z='echo z'

### 7.2 defining an alias: exactly ONE argument processed
    input:  alias a='echo A' b='echo B'; alias
    stdout: a='echo A'
    (the second argument b='echo B' is SILENTLY IGNORED)
No name validation:
    input:  alias 1x='echo bad'; 1x
    stdout: bad
Redefinition overwrites:
    input:  alias x='echo hi'; alias x='echo bye'; x
    stdout: bye
Empty value is a PARSE ERROR (whole program rejected, exit 255):
    input:  alias x=; alias x; alias
    stderr:
nsh: parse error:  --> 1:9
  |
1 | alias x=; alias x; alias
  |         ^---
  |
  = expected literal_span, tilde_span, any_string_span, any_char_span, command_span, proc_subst_direction, backtick_span, expr_span, param_ex_span, param_span, double_quoted_span, or single_quoted_span
    exit: 255

### 7.3 `alias name` (query) — NOT SUPPORTED, always an error
    input:  alias ll            (even when ll IS defined)
    stderr (exact, trailing newline after last line):
nsh: alias:  --> 1:1
  |
1 | ll
  | ^---
  |
  = expected alias
    exit/status: 1   ($? = 1; script continues)
    input:  alias --help        -> same error shape with `--help` in the text.

### 7.4 alias EXPANSION semantics
- Expansion happens at EXECUTION time, not parse time:
      input:  alias x='echo hi'; unalias x; x      (unalias doesn't exist; x runs)
      stdout: hi
- Value is split on whitespace into LITERAL words; the first word replaces the
  command word, the rest are prepended as arguments. NO re-parsing:
      input:  alias e='echo $HOME'; e
      stdout: $HOME                    ($ is NOT re-expanded!)
      input:  alias w='echo one; echo two'; w
      stdout: one; echo two            (';' is a literal word, not a separator)
      input:  alias x="echo 'q u'"; x
      stdout: 'q u'                    (quotes are literal characters)
- User arguments are appended:
      input:  alias e='echo hello'; e world
      stdout: hello world
- Aliases override builtins:
      input:  alias echo='echo E'; echo hi
      stdout: E hi
      input:  alias cd='echo NOCD'; cd /tmp; pwd
      stdout: NOCD /tmp
              /workspace               (cd never ran)
- Expansion is SINGLE-SHOT (no recursion):
      input:  alias a='echo hi'; alias b=a; b
      stderr: nsh: command not found `a'      exit: 1
      input:  alias x='x y'; x
      stderr: nsh: command not found `x'      exit: 1
- Only the command word is expanded, not arguments:
      input:  alias ll='ls'; echo ll
      stdout: ll
- Works in any command position (after ';', in pipelines):
      input:  alias ll='ls'; echo piped | ll >/dev/null; echo rc=$?
      stdout: rc= 0

RULES (alias):
- `alias` => list all, format `name='value'`, one per line, nondeterministic order.
- `alias NAME=VALUE` (single arg only; extra args ignored) => define, exit 0.
- anything else (bare name, --help, ...) => error `nsh: alias:  --> 1:1 ... = expected alias`, status 1.
- expansion: execution-time, whitespace-split literal words, single-shot,
  command position only, user args appended.

## 10. Related quirks observed while probing (context for the messages above)

- **Unquoted `$`-expansion introduces word boundaries**: `false; echo rc=$?`
  prints `rc= 1` (two words `rc=` and `1`, joined by echo's space), while
  `echo "rc=$?"` prints `rc=1`. Same for `X=ab; echo pre$X` -> `pre ab`.
  This affects how statuses appear in probe outputs above ("rc= 1" etc.).
- **`||` is broken**: the right-hand side of `||` runs UNCONDITIONALLY.
      true || echo Y   -> prints Y
      false || echo Y  -> prints Y
  `&&` behaves normally (true && echo X -> X; false && echo X -> nothing).
- Parse errors (whole `-c` string rejected before anything runs) print
  `nsh: parse error:  --> ...` to stderr and exit 255.
- `command not found` message: `nsh: command not found \`NAME'` on stderr,
  status 1, execution continues.
- clap-style builtin usage errors print to stderr, set `$?`=1, and execution
  continues with the next command. Error prefix varies per builtin:
  `nsh: unset: error: ...`, `nsh: set: error: ...`, but `shift: error: ...`
  (no `nsh: ` prefix for shift).

When a builtin error occurs mid-script, the error is printed, `$?` is set (usually 1),

## 1. export

### 1.1 `export` with no arguments
    input:  export
    stdout: (empty)
    stderr: (empty)
    exit:   0
Prints NOTHING (no `declare -x` listing, no variable list). Also true when
variables have been exported earlier (`export A=1 B=2; export` still prints nothing).

### 1.2 `export A=1 B=2` (multiple assignments)
    input:  export A=1 B=2; sh -c "echo [$A][$B]"
    stdout: [1][2]
    exit:   0
Multiple `NAME=VALUE` arguments are all processed.

### 1.3 `export A` (mark existing variable)
    input:  A=5; export A; sh -c "echo child=[$A]"
    stdout: child=[5]
    exit:   0

### 1.4 `export NONEXISTENT` (no such variable)
    input:  export NEWVAR; env | grep NEWVAR; echo grep_rc=$?
    stdout: grep_rc= 1
    exit:   0
Silently does nothing; no variable (not even an empty one) is created.

### 1.5 NO name validation — invalid names are silently accepted and exported
    input:  export 1BAD=2; env | grep 1BAD
    stdout: 1BAD=2
    exit:   0
    input:  export BAD-NAME=3; env | grep BAD
    stdout: BAD-NAME=3
    exit:   0
No error message, exit 0. (Note: `echo "[$1BAD]"` prints `[2]` because `$1` is
positional param 1 (empty) followed by literal text — unrelated to export.)

### 1.6 Flags are silently ignored
    input:  export -n A=1; echo "A=$A"      -> stdout: A=1        (A exported normally)
    input:  export -z A=1; echo "A=$A"      -> stdout: A=1        (unknown flag also ignored)
    input:  export -- A=1; echo "A=$A"      -> stdout: A=1        (-- consumed)
    input:  export -n                      -> no output, exit 0
    input:  export --help                  -> no output, exit 0   (NOT treated as help!)
All exit 0, no output, no error. Any `-x`/`--xxx` token is simply dropped.

### 1.7 **export is effectively a NO-OP: ALL shell variables are visible to children**
    input:  A=5; sh -c "echo noexport=[$A]"
    stdout: noexport=[5]
    exit:   0
A plain (never exported) shell variable appears in a child process's environment.
So `export` has no observable effect at all; every shell variable is passed to
external commands.

### 1.8 unset after export removes it from the environment
    input:  export A=1; unset A; sh -c "echo afterunset=[$A]"; echo "shell=[$A]"
    stdout: afterunset=[]
            shell=[]
    exit:   0

RULES (export):
- exit status always 0.
- never prints anything, never errors.
- parses args: tokens starting with `-` are discarded; `NAME=VALUE` tokens assign
  (any byte string as NAME, no validation); bare `NAME` tokens are no-ops unless
  the variable exists (and even then, no observable difference — see 1.7).
- all shell variables are always passed to child processes' environments.

Uses clap-style argument parsing. Takes EXACTLY ONE argument `<NAME>`.

### 2.1 success

    stdout: []
    exit:   0
Also removes the variable from the environment seen by children (see 1.8).

### 2.2 unset of nonexistent variable
    input:  unset NOPE; echo after
    stdout: after
    exit:   0
No error.

### 2.3 no arguments — clap error (exact stderr, note trailing blank line)

    stderr:

    <NAME>

    unset <NAME>

For more information try --help

FLAGS:

ARGS:

### 4.5 `shift --help` (stderr, exit 1, stdout empty; `<n>` line has 4 trailing spaces)
shift: shift 0.4.2
shift command.

USAGE:
    shift [n]

FLAGS:
    -h, --help       Prints help information
    -V, --version    Prints version information

ARGS:
    <n>    


NOTE: script-level positional params cannot be supplied via the CLI:
`./executable --norc script.sh a b c` fails with
    error: Found argument 'a' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

    USAGE:
        executable --norc

    For more information try --help
(exit 1). So `shift` is only observable inside functions in practice.

---

## 5. exit

### 5.1 normal numeric argument
    input:  exit 5        -> no output, process exit code 5
    input:  echo before; exit 3; echo after
    stdout: before        exit: 3   (terminates immediately)
    input:  f() { exit 3; }; f; echo no
    (no output)           exit: 3   (exit inside a function exits the shell)

### 5.2 no argument — ALWAYS exits 0 (NOT the last command's status!)
    input:  false; exit   -> exit code 0
    input:  true;  exit   -> exit code 0
    input:  exit          -> exit code 0

### 5.3 argument is parsed as a Rust i32 (decimal, optional sign, NO spaces/junk)
    exit 300      -> 44   (value mod 256 via process exit)
    exit 256      -> 0
    exit 65536    -> 0
    exit -1       -> 255
    exit +5       -> 5    (leading '+' accepted)
    exit 08       -> 8    (leading zeros ok)
    exit abc      -> 1    (parse failure: NO message, exit code 1)
    exit 12abc    -> 1
    exit ""       -> 1
    exit " 7"     -> 1    (leading space not allowed)
    exit 0x10     -> 1
    exit 99999999999999999999 -> 1  (i32 overflow)

### 5.4 extra arguments are silently ignored
    input:  exit 1 2      -> exit code 1, no output

RULES (exit):
- `exit [N]`; missing N => 0; unparseable N => 1 (silently); otherwise N as i32,
  process exit code = N mod 256 (OS truncation of negative/large values).
- extra args ignored; never prints anything.

---

## 6. return

### 6.1 inside a function: stops the function, status is ALWAYS 0 (argument IGNORED)
    input:  f() { return; echo NO; }; f; echo "after $?"
    stdout: after 0        (function body stops at return)
    input:  f() { return 7; }; f; echo rc=$?
    stdout: rc= 0          (NOT 7! return's numeric argument has no effect)
    input:  f() { false; return; }; f; echo rc=$?
    stdout: rc= 0          (even a preceding failure is discarded)
    input:  f() { return 300; }; f; echo rc=$?
    stdout: rc= 0
    input:  f() { return 7; }; f          (as last command)
    exit:   0
(The space in "rc= 0" is the unquoted-expansion word-splitting quirk — see §10.)

### 6.2 grammar: `return` takes nothing or a single unsigned decimal `num`
    input:  f() { return abc; }; f
    stderr:
nsh: parse error:  --> 1:14
  |
1 | f() { return abc; }; f
  |              ^---
  |
  = expected num, and_or_list_sep, or compound_list_sep
    exit: 255  (whole program rejected at parse time)
    input:  f() { return -1; }; f   -> parse error, same shape ("expected num, ...")
    input:  f() { return 1 2; }; f  -> parse error:
      = expected and_or_list_sep or compound_list_sep   (at the second token)
    `return 08` is accepted (leading zeros fine), status still 0.

### 6.3 OUTSIDE a function: PANIC (top level of -c, script file, or sourced file)
    input:  return            (also: return 5; also `return 3` inside a sourced file)
    stdout: (whatever ran before, e.g. `echo before; return` prints "before")
    stderr (first two lines, deterministic):
nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:133:14:
unexpected Return
    ...then a Rust backtrace (NONDETERMINISTIC addresses; each line prefixed
    with "nsh:    " — the panic hook prefixes all stderr with "nsh: ")...
    ...then a blank line and the final deterministic line:
nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues
    exit: 101
Commands after `return` do not run. (Also writes a log to ~/.nsh.log.)

RULES (return):
- in function: unwinds the function, sets status 0, ignores its argument.
- outside function: process panics with exit 101.

---

## 7. alias

Custom-parsed (NOT clap). Takes ZERO or ONE argument.

### 7.1 `alias` with no args — list all aliases
    input:  alias
    stdout: (empty)            exit: 0     (when no aliases defined)
    input:  alias ll='ls -l'; alias
    stdout: ll='ls -l'
    exit:   0
Format per line:  NAME='VALUE'\n   (raw value between single quotes, NO escaping)
    input:  alias x="echo 'q u'"; alias
    stdout: x='echo 'q u''
**ORDER IS NONDETERMINISTIC** (Rust HashMap iteration). Two identical runs:
    run1: z='echo z' / m='echo m' / a='echo a'
    run2: m='echo m' / a='echo a' / z='echo z'

### 7.2 defining an alias: exactly ONE argument processed
    input:  alias a='echo A' b='echo B'; alias
    stdout: a='echo A'
    (the second argument b='echo B' is SILENTLY IGNORED)
No name validation:
    input:  alias 1x='echo bad'; 1x
    stdout: bad
Redefinition overwrites:
    input:  alias x='echo hi'; alias x='echo bye'; x
    stdout: bye
Empty value is a PARSE ERROR (whole program rejected, exit 255):
    input:  alias x=; alias x; alias
    stderr:
nsh: parse error:  --> 1:9
  |
1 | alias x=; alias x; alias
  |         ^---
  |
  = expected literal_span, tilde_span, any_string_span, any_char_span, command_span, proc_subst_direction, backtick_span, expr_span, param_ex_span, param_span, double_quoted_span, or single_quoted_span
    exit: 255

### 7.3 `alias name` (query) — NOT SUPPORTED, always an error
    input:  alias ll            (even when ll IS defined)
    stderr (exact, trailing newline after last line):
nsh: alias:  --> 1:1
  |
1 | ll
  | ^---
  |
  = expected alias
    exit/status: 1   ($? = 1; script continues)
    input:  alias --help        -> same error shape with `--help` in the text.

### 7.4 alias EXPANSION semantics
- Expansion happens at EXECUTION time, not parse time:
      input:  alias x='echo hi'; unalias x; x      (unalias doesn't exist; x runs)
      stdout: hi
- Value is split on whitespace into LITERAL words; the first word replaces the
  command word, the rest are prepended as arguments. NO re-parsing:
      input:  alias e='echo $HOME'; e
      stdout: $HOME                    ($ is NOT re-expanded!)
      input:  alias w='echo one; echo two'; w
      stdout: one; echo two            (';' is a literal word, not a separator)
      input:  alias x="echo 'q u'"; x
      stdout: 'q u'                    (quotes are literal characters)
- User arguments are appended:
      input:  alias e='echo hello'; e world
      stdout: hello world
- Aliases override builtins:
      input:  alias echo='echo E'; echo hi
      stdout: E hi
      input:  alias cd='echo NOCD'; cd /tmp; pwd
      stdout: NOCD /tmp
              /workspace               (cd never ran)
- Expansion is SINGLE-SHOT (no recursion):
      input:  alias a='echo hi'; alias b=a; b
      stderr: nsh: command not found `a'      exit: 1
      input:  alias x='x y'; x
      stderr: nsh: command not found `x'      exit: 1
- Only the command word is expanded, not arguments:
      input:  alias ll='ls'; echo ll
      stdout: ll
- Works in any command position (after ';', in pipelines):
      input:  alias ll='ls'; echo piped | ll >/dev/null; echo rc=$?
      stdout: rc= 0

RULES (alias):
- `alias` => list all, format `name='value'`, one per line, nondeterministic order.
- `alias NAME=VALUE` (single arg only; extra args ignored) => define, exit 0.
- anything else (bare name, --help, ...) => error `nsh: alias:  --> 1:1 ... = expected alias`, status 1.
- expansion: execution-time, whitespace-split literal words, single-shot,
  command position only, user args appended.

---

## 8. unalias — **NOT A BUILTIN AT ALL**

    input:  unalias
    stderr: nsh: command not found `unalias'
    exit:   1
    input:  alias x='echo hi'; unalias x; x
    stdout: hi                     (alias survives)
    stderr: nsh: command not found `unalias'
    exit:   0                      (last command was x)
    input:  unalias -a
    stderr: nsh: command not found `unalias'
    exit:   1
There is NO way to remove an alias. (Note: the general "command not found"
status in nsh is 1, and the message is  nsh: command not found `NAME'  )

---

## 9. local and readonly

### 9.1 local — IS supported (a special form), only inside functions
    input:  x=global; f() { local x=inner; echo "in=$x"; }; f; echo "out=$x"
    stdout: in=inner
            out=global
    exit:   0                (real function scoping)
    input:  f() { local x; echo "[$x]"; }; f
    stdout: []
    exit:   0                (local without value => empty)
    input:  local x=1        (at top level)
    stderr: nsh: local variable can only be used in a function
    exit:   1
    input:  local            (bare)
    stderr:
nsh: parse error:  --> 1:6
  |
1 | local
  |      ^---
  |
  = expected var_name
    exit: 255                (parse error — local is grammar, not a builtin)

### 9.2 readonly — NOT a builtin
    input:  readonly A=1
    stderr: nsh: command not found `readonly'
    exit:   1
There are no readonly variables; `unset` never fails for that reason.

---

## 10. Related quirks observed while probing (context for the messages above)

- **Unquoted `$`-expansion introduces word boundaries**: `false; echo rc=$?`
  prints `rc= 1` (two words `rc=` and `1`, joined by echo's space), while
  `echo "rc=$?"` prints `rc=1`. Same for `X=ab; echo pre$X` -> `pre ab`.
  This affects how statuses appear in probe outputs above ("rc= 1" etc.).
- **`||` is broken**: the right-hand side of `||` runs UNCONDITIONALLY.
      true || echo Y   -> prints Y
      false || echo Y  -> prints Y
  `&&` behaves normally (true && echo X -> X; false && echo X -> nothing).
- Parse errors (whole `-c` string rejected before anything runs) print
  `nsh: parse error:  --> ...` to stderr and exit 255.
- `command not found` message: `nsh: command not found \`NAME'` on stderr,
  status 1, execution continues.
- clap-style builtin usage errors print to stderr, set `$?`=1, and execution
  continues with the next command. Error prefix varies per builtin:
  `nsh: unset: error: ...`, `nsh: set: error: ...`, but `shift: error: ...`
  (no `nsh: ` prefix for shift).

payload.resultSummary:
Spec written to `/workspace/specs/builtins_vars.md` (589 lines, all behaviors captured with exact input/stdout/stderr/exit codes plus inferred rules). Most important/surprising findings:

- **`unalias` is not a builtin at all** — `nsh: command not found \`unalias'`; aliases can never be removed. `readonly` is also absent, but `local` IS supported (real function scoping; top-level use gives `nsh: local variable can only be used in a function`).
- **`export` is a complete no-op**: it prints nothing with no args, silently accepts invalid names (`export 1BAD=2` exports `1BAD=2` to the environment!), ignores all flags including `--help`, and — critically — **all shell variables are passed to child processes even without export**.
- **`return N` inside a function always sets status 0** (argument ignored); outside a function it **panics** (`nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:133:14: unexpected Return`, backtrace, exit 101).
- **`exit` with no arg exits 0** (not last status); arg parsed as Rust i32 — junk/empty/`" 7"` silently exit 1, `+5`→5, values mod 256.
- **`set` accepts only `-e`/`-n`/`-u`** (all functional; `-n` no-execs the rest but parsing still happens upfront); `set` prints nothing, `set -- a b` is rejected so positional params are unsettable. `set --help`/`-V` go to stderr with exit 1.
- **`alias name` (query) errors** (`nsh: alias: --> 1:1 ... expected alias`); only ONE `name=value` arg processed per call; listing order is **nondeterministic** (HashMap); expansion is execution-time, single-shot, whitespace-split literal words with no re-parsing (`$HOME`, `;`, quotes stay literal).
- Builtin clap errors print usage to stderr, set `$?`=1, and execution **continues**; error prefixes are inconsistent: `nsh: unset:`/`nsh: set:` vs bare `shift:`.
- Bonus quirks documented: `||` runs its RHS unconditionally (broken), and unquoted `$?`-style expansions split into separate words (`echo rc=$?` → `rc= 1`).

payload.resultSummary:
Spec written to `/workspace/specs/parser_errors.md` (345 lines), with exact byte-level format, a large input→error table, rule-name inventory/ordering, panic cases, and inferred grammar rules.

Key findings:

- **Format**: pest-style rendering prefixed with `nsh: parse error: ` (hence the double space before `-->`); gutter width grows with line-number digits; marker is always exactly `^---`; columns count Unicode chars not bytes; tabs in the source line are reproduced as tabs in the marker line; long lines are never truncated. Always stderr, always exit 255.
- **Whole-input parsing**: the entire `-c` string / script / `eval` / `source` text is parsed before anything executes — one error anywhere means zero commands run. `eval` errors show the eval'd text with a trailing space appended.
- **Rule names mapped**: ~28 pest rule names (`EOI, word, escaped_char, ..., param_op, var_name, heredoc_marker, redirect_to_fd, elif_part, else_part, arith_for_exprs, comp_op, assign_op, arith_op, factor_op, ...`), with observed declaration order (needed to reproduce `expected` list ordering exactly).
- **Panics (exit 101) instead of parse errors**: `<&`/`>&` without a numeric fd and `>&-` (parser.rs:868 ParseIntError unwrap), heredoc with missing body / two heredocs on one line (parser.rs:1326 index OOB), `>(...)` (expand.rs:238 `not implemented`). Full backtrace printed (addresses nondeterministic) plus a "Something went wrong… GitHub" footer; ANSI-colored on tty.
- **PEG backtracking quirks**: bad arithmetic like `$((1+))` doesn't parse-error — it backtracks into nested command substitution and fails at runtime (`command not found '1+'`, glob `no matches`). No brace expansion (`{a,b}` is a parse error), no `>|`, `&>`, `<<<`, quoted heredoc markers, `case (` patterns, `function`, `select`, `until` (plain command!), `!`/`time` keywords.
- **Other quirks**: `<<-` does not strip tabs when matching the terminator; multiple `;` are legal but `;;` isn't; `for i do`/`for i; do` rejected (`in` or `((...))` required); `case` arm bodies require `;;`; `while do done` hangs forever silently; non-tty stdin is never executed — just `nsh: warning: stdout is not a tty` and exit 0 (so incomplete-stdin continuation can't be probed).

mkdir -p /workspace/specs && cat > /workspace/specs/expansion.md <<'SPEC_EOF'
# nsh 0.4.2 — Expansion behavior spec (parameter, arithmetic, command substitution, tilde, field splitting)

Characterized by black-box probing of `/workspace/executable` (always run as
`HOME=/tmp/nshprobe ./executable --norc -c '...'`, stdout/stderr captured separately).
Unless noted, examples show: input → stdout, stderr, exit code.

NONDETERMINISM NOTES:
- `$$`, `$!`, and all PIDs/addresses in Rust panic backtraces are nondeterministic.
- Panic backtraces (full `nsh:    0: 0x...` frames) are printed on stderr after the panic
  line whenever the shell panics; the exact addresses vary run to run. They are omitted below
  and marked `[backtrace follows]`. The panic trailer line is always:

adjacent literal text in the same word. Quoted expansion concatenates normally.

`echo $((2*3+4*5))`  → `26`
`echo $((1+2<4))`    → `1`
`echo $((2*3<7))`    → `1`

`x=5; echo $((x--)); echo "x=$x"`     → `4` / `x=4`   (same: returns new value)

`echo $((x++)); echo "x=[$x]"`        → `1` / `x=[1]`  (unset x → 0, then incremented; var created)
`x=abc; echo $((x++)); echo "x=[$x]"` → `1` / `x=[1]`

`echo $((1<2)) $((2<=2)) $((3>2)) $((3>=4)) $((1==1)) $((1!=2))` → `1 1 1 0 1 1`
`echo $(( 1 + 2 ))`                → `3`         (whitespace fine)
`echo $(((1+2)*3))`                → `9`         (nested parens)
`echo $((2 * (3 + 4)))`            → `14`

ASSOCIATIVITY BUG (non-standard, must reproduce): binary operator chains are RIGHT-associative
(precedence levels are normal, but within/across a chain it parses right-recursively):
`echo $((10-2-3))`   → `11`    (i.e. 10-(2-3), POSIX would give 5)
`echo $((20-10+5))`  → `5`     (i.e. 20-(10+5))
`echo $((2-3+4))`    → `-5`    (i.e. 2-(3+4))
`echo $((100/10/2))` → `20`    (i.e. 100/(10/2))
`echo $((6/2*3))`    → `1`     (i.e. 6/(2*3), POSIX would give 9)
`echo $((2*3/2))`    → `2`     (i.e. 2*(3/2)=2*1; POSIX would give 3)
`echo $((1<2==1))`   → `0`     (i.e. 1<(2==1))
But normal precedence still applies when it must:
`echo $((1+2*3))`    → `7`
`echo $((1+2*3+4))`  → `11`
`echo $((2*3+4*5))`  → `26`
`echo $((1+2<4))`    → `1`
`echo $((2*3<7))`    → `1`

Variables inside arithmetic:
`x=5; echo $((x+1))`        → `6`
`echo $((UNSETVAR+1))`      → `1`        (unset var → 0)
`x=abc; echo $((x+1))`      → `1`        (non-numeric var → 0)
`x="3+4"; echo $((x+1))`    → `1`        (var values are NOT recursively parsed as expressions)
`x=-5; echo $((x+10))`      → `5`        (negative values parse)
`n=010; echo $((n+1))`      → `11`       (leading zeros = DECIMAL, not octal)

Assignment and inc/dec (SIDE EFFECTS PERSIST in the parent shell):
`x=5; echo $((x=9)); echo "x=$x"`     → `9` / `x=9`
`echo $((x=2+3)); echo "x=$x"`        → `5` / `x=5`
`echo $((a=b=3)); echo "a=$a b=$b"`   → `3` / `a=3 b=3`   (chained, right-assoc)
`x=1; y=2; echo $((x=y)); echo "x=$x"` → `2` / `x=2`
`x=5; echo $((x++)); echo "x=$x"`     → `6` / `x=6`   (POSTFIX SYNTAX, PREFIX SEMANTICS:
                                                        returns the NEW value, increments var)
`x=5; echo $((x--)); echo "x=$x"`     → `4` / `x=4`   (same: returns new value)
`x=5; echo $((x++ + 10)); echo "x=$x"` → `16` / `x=6` (x++ evaluated as 6)
`x=5; echo $((x ++)); echo "x=$x"`    → `6` (space before ++ ok)
`echo $((x++)); echo "x=[$x]"`        → `1` / `x=[1]`  (unset x → 0, then incremented; var created)
`x=abc; echo $((x++)); echo "x=[$x]"` → `1` / `x=[1]`

`$((007))`→7, `$((00))`→0). Arithmetic WRAPS on i32 overflow (release-mode wrapping):
`echo $((2147483647+1))`  → `-2147483648`
`echo $((2147483647*2))`  → `-2`
But a LITERAL larger than i32::MAX (or < i32::MIN via unary minus) PANICS at parse time:
`echo $((2147483648))`    → exit 101, stderr:
    nsh: panicked at src/parser.rs:492:67:
    called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: ParseIntError { kind: PosOverflow }
    [backtrace follows]
`echo $((-2147483648))`   → same panic (literal 2147483648 overflows before negation)
`echo $((9223372036854775807+1))` → same panic

DIVISION BY ZERO panics and KILLS THE WHOLE SHELL (remaining commands do not run):
`echo before; echo $((10/0)); echo after` → exit 101, stdout `before\n`, stderr:
    nsh: panicked at src/eval.rs:38:47:
    attempt to divide by zero
    [backtrace follows]

EMPTY arithmetic: `echo $(( ))` → empty line, no error; `echo $(())` → empty line, no error.
UNCLOSED: `echo $((1+2` → exit 255, stderr:
    nsh: parse error:  --> 1:12
      |
    1 | echo $((1+2
      |            ^---
      |
      = expected comp_op, arith_op, factor_op, word, escaped_char, unescaped_char, literal_span, any_string_span, any_char_span, command_span, proc_subst_direction, backtick_span, expr_span, param_ex_span, param_span, double_quoted_span, single_quoted_span, redirect_direction, heredoc, and_or_list_sep, or compound_list_sep

### 5.2 UNSUPPORTED operators → SILENT FALLBACK TO COMMAND SUBSTITUTION
If the `$((...)` content fails to parse as a supported arithmetic expression, nsh re-parses the
whole thing as command substitution of a subshell `( ... )`. I.e. `$((STUFF))` → `$((STUFF))`
is executed like `$( (STUFF) )`. Consequences: the text is run as a COMMAND in a subshell,
output is captured (usually none), side effects do NOT persist, and diagnostics come from
normal command execution.

Unsupported: `%`, `**`, `<<`, `>>`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `&&`, `||`, `!`, ternary `?:`,

`echo $((8 % 3))`  → stdout empty; stderr `nsh: command not found \`8'` (ran `8` with args `% 3`)
`echo $((2 ** 8))` → stderr `nsh: command not found \`2'`
`echo $((2**8))`   → PANIC in the subshell, exit still 0; stderr:

    failed to glob: PatternError { pos: 0, msg: "recursive wildcards must form a single path component" }
    [backtrace follows]   (`2**8` treated as a glob pattern; `**` glob panic)
`echo $((1<<3))`   → PANIC in subshell, exit 0; stderr:
    nsh: panicked at src/process.rs:367:17:
    internal error: entered unreachable code
    [backtrace follows]   (`1 <<3` = command `1` with heredoc)
`echo $((16>>2))`  → stdout empty, NO error (command `16` would... actually ran `16 >>2`: redirect

                     RE-VERIFY if reimplementing exactly.)
`echo $((5&3))`    → stderr `nsh: command not found \`5'` and `nsh: command not found \`3'`

`echo $((5|3))`    → stderr `nsh: command not found \`5'` + `nsh: command not found \`3'` (pipeline)
`echo $((5^3))`    → stderr `nsh: command not found \`5^3'`
`echo $((~5))`     → stderr:

`echo $((1&&0))`   → stderr `nsh: command not found \`1'` (short-circuit)
`echo $((1||0))`   → stderr `nsh: command not found \`1'` then `nsh: command not found \`0'`
`echo $((!0))`     → stderr `nsh: command not found \`!0'`
`echo $((1,2,3))`  → stderr `nsh: command not found \`1,2,3'`
`echo $((1.5+1))`  → stderr `nsh: command not found \`1.5+1'`

args.command:
mkdir -p /workspace/specs && cat > /workspace/specs/lexer.md <<'SPEC_EOF'
# nsh 0.4.2 — Lexer / Tokenization Behavior Spec

All behaviors below were observed by running `/workspace/executable` (nsh 0.4.2)
through its normal CLI only. Unless noted otherwise, tests used:

    export HOME=/tmp/nshprobe        # isolated HOME
    ./executable --norc -c '<input>' # stdout/stderr captured separately

Conventions: `exit=` is the process exit code. `--stdout--` / `--stderr--` are
byte-exact unless noted. `\n` in input descriptions means a literal newline byte.
Nondeterministic values (PIDs, backtrace addresses) are marked [nondeterministic].

General exit-code conventions observed:
- Successful run: exit 0 (or status of last command).
- Parse error: message `nsh: parse error: ...` on stderr, exit 255.
- Internal panic (Rust): message `nsh: panicked at src/...` + backtrace on stderr, exit 101.
- Runtime errors (command not found, glob no-match, redirect failure): exit 1.

========================================================================
1. WHITESPACE AND LINE STRUCTURE
========================================================================

Word separators: space, tab, newline, and carriage return (\r).
Vertical tab (\v) and form feed (\f) are NOT whitespace — they stay literal in words.

- Input: `echo a\tb`  (tab)        → stdout `a b\n`, exit 0
- Input: `echo a\vb`  (literal VT) → stdout bytes `a \v b \n`, exit 0 (one arg "a\vb")
- Input: `echo a\fb`  (literal FF) → stdout bytes `a \f b \n`, exit 0
- Script file containing `echo a\rb\n` (\r = CR):
  → stdout `a b\n`, exit 0  (CR acts as word separator: two args "a" "b")
- Leading/trailing whitespace ignored: `  echo a  ` → `a\n`, exit 0.
- Runs of separators collapse: `echo  a   b` → `a b\n`.
- Newline is a command separator like `;`:
  -c 'echo a\necho b' → stdout `a\nb\n`, exit 0.
- Empty input `-c ''` → no output, exit 0. Whitespace-only input → no output, exit 0.
- Multiple consecutive `;` are ALLOWED (empty commands skipped):
  `echo a; ;echo b` → `a\nb\n`, exit 0.  `echo a ; ; echo b` → same.
  `;` alone → no output, exit 0.
- Multiple `&` likewise: `echo x & & echo y` → `x\ny\n`, exit 0.

Newline continuation after binary operators is allowed (grammar explicitly expects
`normal_newline or command` after `|`, `&&`, `||`):
- `true &&\necho cont` → `cont\n`, exit 0
- `echo a |\ncat` → `a\n`, exit 0
- `echo a ||\necho b` → `a\nb\n` (see || semantics note in §9)
- `echo a &\necho b` → `a\nb\n`, exit 0

========================================================================
2. COMMENTS
========================================================================

`#` starts a comment ONLY at the beginning of a word (i.e. after whitespace,
after an operator, or at line start). Mid-word `#` is literal. The comment runs
to end of line.

- `echo a#b`        → stdout `a#b\n`, exit 0          (# mid-word is literal)
- `echo #b`         → stdout `\n`, exit 0             (whole rest is comment)
- `echo a ;#comment`→ stdout `a\n`, exit 0            (# after operator = comment)
- `echo a;# comment`→ stdout `a\n`, exit 0
- `echo x; #comment to end` → `x\n`, exit 0
- `a#b=c`           → stderr `nsh: command not found \`a#b=c'`, exit 1
- `echo a&#z` (as part of `echo x;echo y&#z`) → works; comment after `&`.
- `(#cmt\necho inpar)` → `inpar\n`, exit 0  (comment inside subshell)
- After a quote, `#` is mid-word and stays literal:
  - `echo "x"#c` → stdout `x#c\n`
  - `echo ''#c`  → stdout `#c\n`   (word already started by empty quotes)
  - `echo "#"x`  → stdout `#x\n`
- `#` immediately after a redirect operator still starts a comment, leaving the
  redirect without a target → parse error:
  - `echo a >#f` → exit 255, stderr:
      nsh: parse error:  --> 1:11
        |
      1 | echo a >#f
        |           ^---
        |
        = expected word or redirect_to_fd

========================================================================
3. QUOTING
========================================================================

--- 3.1 Single quotes ---
Everything literal until the next `'`; no escapes, no expansions; may span newlines.
- `echo 'a b'`      → `a b\n`
- `echo 'a"b'`      → `a"b\n`
- `echo '$HOME'`    → `$HOME\n`
- `echo 'multi\nline'` (literal newline inside) → stdout `multi\nline\n`, exit 0
- Unterminated: `echo 'unterminated` → exit 255, stderr:
    nsh: parse error:  --> 1:19
      |
    1 | echo 'unterminated
      |                   ^---
      |
      = expected literal_in_single_quoted_span
- `echo it's` (apostrophe opens a quote) → exit 255, same "expected
  literal_in_single_quoted_span" error at 1:10.

--- 3.2 Double quotes ---
Literal until closing `"`; `$`, backticks, `$(...)`, `${...}`, `$((...))` are
expanded inside. May span newlines (newline kept literally).
- `echo "a b"`     → `a b\n`
- `echo "a|b&c;d"` → `a|b&c;d\n`  (operators literal inside quotes)
- `echo "a\nb"` (literal newline) → `a\nb\n`
- `echo "tab\tinside"` (literal TAB) → tab byte preserved.
- Backslash inside double quotes is special ONLY before `$`, `"`, `` ` ``, `\`.
  Before any other char (including newline!) the backslash stays LITERAL:
  - `echo "a\$HOME"` → `a$HOME\n`
  - `echo "a\"b"`    → `a"b\n`
  - `echo "a\\b"`    → `a\b\n`   (one backslash)
  - `echo "a\`b"`    → `a`+"`"+`b` → `a`b\n`
  - `echo "a\xb"`    → `a\xb\n`  (backslash kept — NOT POSIX)
  - `echo "a\!b"`    → `a\!b\n`
  - `echo "a\<NEWLINE>b"` → bytes `a \ <newline> b \n` — BOTH backslash and
    newline kept literally (NOT POSIX; POSIX removes both).
- `echo "a\"` (escaped quote, then EOF) → exit 255:
    nsh: parse error:  --> 1:10
      |
    1 | echo "a\"
      |          ^---
      |
      = expected command_span, backtick_span, expr_span, param_ex_span, param_span, or literal_in_double_quoted_span
- `echo "` → exit 255, same error at 1:7.

--- 3.3 Backslash outside quotes ---
Backslash escapes the next character; the next char becomes literal (special or
not — `\x` → `x`). Observed:
- `echo a\ b`   → `a b\n`   (escaped space joins the word; ONE arg "a b")
- `echo a\<TAB>b` → bytes `a \t b \n` (one arg with literal tab)
- `echo \a`     → `a\n`
- `echo \x`     → `x\n`
- `echo \\`     → `\n`... precisely: stdout bytes `\ \n` (one backslash)
- `echo \$HOME` → `$HOME\n`
- `echo \"`     → `"\n`
- `echo \'x`    → `'x\n`
- `echo \#;` (input `echo \#\;`) → `#;\n`  (escaped # does NOT start a comment)
- `echo \|\&`   → `|&\n`    (escaped operators are literal word chars)
- `echo \*`     → `*\n`     (escaped * does NOT glob)
- `echo \~`     → `~\n`     (no tilde expansion)
- `echo \``... input `echo \`x\`` → `` `x` `` + `\n` (escaped backticks literal)
- `echo a\\b`   → `a\b\n`
- `echo\ echo`  → stderr `nsh: command not found \`echo echo'`, exit 1
  (escaped space inside command-name word)

BACKSLASH-NEWLINE (non-POSIX!):
- If the escaped newline is the FIRST element of a word (word not yet started),
  it acts as a line continuation and is REMOVED:
  - `echo a \<NL>b`   → `a b\n` (two args "a" "b"; nothing left behind)
  - `echo \<NL>hello`  → `hello\n`
  - `\<NL>echo hi`     → `hi\n`  (continuation at line start)
- If the word has already started (any preceding content, even empty quotes),
  the escaped newline becomes a LITERAL NEWLINE BYTE inside the word:
  - `echo a\<NL>b`        → bytes `a \n b \n`   (one arg "a\nb")
  - `echo a\<NL>\<NL>b`   → bytes `a \n \n b \n` (one arg "a\n\nb")
  - `echo a\<NL> b`       → bytes `a \n   b \n`  (args "a\n" and "b")
  - `echo ""\<NL>x`       → bytes `\n x \n`      (one arg "\nx")
  - `echo x""\<NL>y`      → bytes `x \n y \n`
  - script file `echo x\<NL>` (EOF after newline) → bytes `x \n \n` (arg "x\n")
- Lone trailing backslash at EOF (no newline after it): the backslash is silently
  dropped, but the word still exists (possibly empty):
  - `echo a\`  → `a\n`
  - `echo \`   → `\n`         (one empty arg)
  - `echo a \` → bytes `a   \n` i.e. `a \n` — args "a" and "" (trailing space!)

--- 3.4 Adjacent quote/literal concatenation ---
Quoted and unquoted LITERAL fragments concatenate into one word:
- `echo a'b'"c"d`   → `abcd\n`
- `echo 'it''s'`    → `its\n`
- `echo a''b`       → `ab\n`

  (single space between two empty args).
- BUT see §4: an unquoted `$var` / `$(...)` / `` `...` `` fragment does NOT

# nsh 0.4.2 — Lexer / Tokenization Behavior Spec

All behaviors below were observed by running `/workspace/executable` (nsh 0.4.2)
through its normal CLI only. Unless noted otherwise, tests used:

    export HOME=/tmp/nshprobe        # isolated HOME
    ./executable --norc -c '<input>' # stdout/stderr captured separately

Conventions: `exit=` is the process exit code. `--stdout--` / `--stderr--` are
byte-exact unless noted. `\n` in input descriptions means a literal newline byte.
Nondeterministic values (PIDs, backtrace addresses) are marked [nondeterministic].

General exit-code conventions observed:
- Successful run: exit 0 (or status of last command).
- Parse error: message `nsh: parse error: ...` on stderr, exit 255.
- Internal panic (Rust): message `nsh: panicked at src/...` + backtrace on stderr, exit 101.
- Runtime errors (command not found, glob no-match, redirect failure): exit 1.

========================================================================
1. WHITESPACE AND LINE STRUCTURE
========================================================================

Word separators: space, tab, newline, and carriage return (\r).
Vertical tab (\v) and form feed (\f) are NOT whitespace — they stay literal in words.

- Input: `echo a\tb`  (tab)        → stdout `a b\n`, exit 0
- Input: `echo a\vb`  (literal VT) → stdout bytes `a \v b \n`, exit 0 (one arg "a\vb")
- Input: `echo a\fb`  (literal FF) → stdout bytes `a \f b \n`, exit 0
- Script file containing `echo a\rb\n` (\r = CR):
  → stdout `a b\n`, exit 0  (CR acts as word separator: two args "a" "b")
- Leading/trailing whitespace ignored: `  echo a  ` → `a\n`, exit 0.
- Runs of separators collapse: `echo  a   b` → `a b\n`.
- Newline is a command separator like `;`:
  -c 'echo a\necho b' → stdout `a\nb\n`, exit 0.
- Empty input `-c ''` → no output, exit 0. Whitespace-only input → no output, exit 0.
- Multiple consecutive `;` are ALLOWED (empty commands skipped):
  `echo a; ;echo b` → `a\nb\n`, exit 0.  `echo a ; ; echo b` → same.
  `;` alone → no output, exit 0.
- Multiple `&` likewise: `echo x & & echo y` → `x\ny\n`, exit 0.

Newline continuation after binary operators is allowed (grammar explicitly expects
`normal_newline or command` after `|`, `&&`, `||`):
- `true &&\necho cont` → `cont\n`, exit 0
- `echo a |\ncat` → `a\n`, exit 0
- `echo a ||\necho b` → `a\nb\n` (see || semantics note in §9)
- `echo a &\necho b` → `a\nb\n`, exit 0

========================================================================
2. COMMENTS
========================================================================

`#` starts a comment ONLY at the beginning of a word (i.e. after whitespace,
after an operator, or at line start). Mid-word `#` is literal. The comment runs
to end of line.

- `echo a#b`        → stdout `a#b\n`, exit 0          (# mid-word is literal)
- `echo #b`         → stdout `\n`, exit 0             (whole rest is comment)
- `echo a ;#comment`→ stdout `a\n`, exit 0            (# after operator = comment)
- `echo a;# comment`→ stdout `a\n`, exit 0
- `echo x; #comment to end` → `x\n`, exit 0
- `a#b=c`           → stderr `nsh: command not found \`a#b=c'`, exit 1
- `echo a&#z` (as part of `echo x;echo y&#z`) → works; comment after `&`.
- `(#cmt\necho inpar)` → `inpar\n`, exit 0  (comment inside subshell)
- After a quote, `#` is mid-word and stays literal:
  - `echo "x"#c` → stdout `x#c\n`
  - `echo ''#c`  → stdout `#c\n`   (word already started by empty quotes)
  - `echo "#"x`  → stdout `#x\n`
- `#` immediately after a redirect operator still starts a comment, leaving the
  redirect without a target → parse error:
  - `echo a >#f` → exit 255, stderr:
      nsh: parse error:  --> 1:11
        |
      1 | echo a >#f
        |           ^---
        |
        = expected word or redirect_to_fd

========================================================================
3. QUOTING
========================================================================

--- 3.1 Single quotes ---
Everything literal until the next `'`; no escapes, no expansions; may span newlines.
- `echo 'a b'`      → `a b\n`
- `echo 'a"b'`      → `a"b\n`
- `echo '$HOME'`    → `$HOME\n`
- `echo 'multi\nline'` (literal newline inside) → stdout `multi\nline\n`, exit 0
- Unterminated: `echo 'unterminated` → exit 255, stderr:
    nsh: parse error:  --> 1:19
      |
    1 | echo 'unterminated
      |                   ^---
      |
      = expected literal_in_single_quoted_span
- `echo it's` (apostrophe opens a quote) → exit 255, same "expected
  literal_in_single_quoted_span" error at 1:10.

--- 3.2 Double quotes ---
Literal until closing `"`; `$`, backticks, `$(...)`, `${...}`, `$((...))` are
expanded inside. May span newlines (newline kept literally).
- `echo "a b"`     → `a b\n`
- `echo "a|b&c;d"` → `a|b&c;d\n`  (operators literal inside quotes)
- `echo "a\nb"` (literal newline) → `a\nb\n`
- `echo "tab\tinside"` (literal TAB) → tab byte preserved.
- Backslash inside double quotes is special ONLY before `$`, `"`, `` ` ``, `\`.
  Before any other char (including newline!) the backslash stays LITERAL:
  - `echo "a\$HOME"` → `a$HOME\n`
  - `echo "a\"b"`    → `a"b\n`
  - `echo "a\\b"`    → `a\b\n`   (one backslash)
  - `echo "a\`b"`    → `a`+"`"+`b` → `a`b\n`
  - `echo "a\xb"`    → `a\xb\n`  (backslash kept — NOT POSIX)
  - `echo "a\!b"`    → `a\!b\n`
  - `echo "a\<NEWLINE>b"` → bytes `a \ <newline> b \n` — BOTH backslash and
    newline kept literally (NOT POSIX; POSIX removes both).
- `echo "a\"` (escaped quote, then EOF) → exit 255:
    nsh: parse error:  --> 1:10
      |
    1 | echo "a\"
      |          ^---
      |
      = expected command_span, backtick_span, expr_span, param_ex_span, param_span, or literal_in_double_quoted_span
- `echo "` → exit 255, same error at 1:7.

--- 3.3 Backslash outside quotes ---
Backslash escapes the next character; the next char becomes literal (special or
not — `\x` → `x`). Observed:
- `echo a\ b`   → `a b\n`   (escaped space joins the word; ONE arg "a b")
- `echo a\<TAB>b` → bytes `a \t b \n` (one arg with literal tab)
- `echo \a`     → `a\n`
- `echo \x`     → `x\n`
- `echo \\`     → `\n`... precisely: stdout bytes `\ \n` (one backslash)
- `echo \$HOME` → `$HOME\n`
- `echo \"`     → `"\n`
- `echo \'x`    → `'x\n`
- `echo \#;` (input `echo \#\;`) → `#;\n`  (escaped # does NOT start a comment)
- `echo \|\&`   → `|&\n`    (escaped operators are literal word chars)
- `echo \*`     → `*\n`     (escaped * does NOT glob)
- `echo \~`     → `~\n`     (no tilde expansion)
- `echo \``... input `echo \`x\`` → `` `x` `` + `\n` (escaped backticks literal)
- `echo a\\b`   → `a\b\n`
- `echo\ echo`  → stderr `nsh: command not found \`echo echo'`, exit 1
  (escaped space inside command-name word)

BACKSLASH-NEWLINE (non-POSIX!):
- If the escaped newline is the FIRST element of a word (word not yet started),
  it acts as a line continuation and is REMOVED:
  - `echo a \<NL>b`   → `a b\n` (two args "a" "b"; nothing left behind)
  - `echo \<NL>hello`  → `hello\n`
  - `\<NL>echo hi`     → `hi\n`  (continuation at line start)
- If the word has already started (any preceding content, even empty quotes),
  the escaped newline becomes a LITERAL NEWLINE BYTE inside the word:
  - `echo a\<NL>b`        → bytes `a \n b \n`   (one arg "a\nb")
  - `echo a\<NL>\<NL>b`   → bytes `a \n \n b \n` (one arg "a\n\nb")
  - `echo a\<NL> b`       → bytes `a \n   b \n`  (args "a\n" and "b")
  - `echo ""\<NL>x`       → bytes `\n x \n`      (one arg "\nx")
  - `echo x""\<NL>y`      → bytes `x \n y \n`
  - script file `echo x\<NL>` (EOF after newline) → bytes `x \n \n` (arg "x\n")
- Lone trailing backslash at EOF (no newline after it): the backslash is silently
  dropped, but the word still exists (possibly empty):
  - `echo a\`  → `a\n`
  - `echo \`   → `\n`         (one empty arg)
  - `echo a \` → bytes `a   \n` i.e. `a \n` — args "a" and "" (trailing space!)

--- 3.4 Adjacent quote/literal concatenation ---
Quoted and unquoted LITERAL fragments concatenate into one word:
- `echo a'b'"c"d`   → `abcd\n`
- `echo 'it''s'`    → `its\n`
- `echo a''b`       → `ab\n`
- `echo ""x""y`     → `xy\n`
- `printf '<%s>' a""b` → `<ab>` (one word)
- Empty strings are real arguments: `printf '[%s]' ''` → `[]`; `echo '' ''` → ` \n`
  (single space between two empty args).
- BUT see §4: an unquoted `$var` / `$(...)` / `` `...` `` fragment does NOT
  concatenate — it becomes its own word(s).

# nsh 0.4.2 — Core Builtins Spec (echo, printf, test/[, true/false/:, cd, pwd, pushd/popd)

Method: black-box probing of `/workspace/executable --norc -c '...'` with isolated HOME.

IMPORTANT GLOBAL QUIRK affecting all examples below:
nsh parses `WORD = VALUE` (spaces around `=` allowed, no space required) at the START of a
simple command as a variable assignment. E.g. `test = a` NEVER runs test; it sets shell
variable `test=a` and exits 0 silently. `foo = hello world` sets foo=hello only for the
command `world` (which then fails: "nsh: command not found `world'", rc=1; foo unset after).
`echo x= a` is a hard parse error (rc=255): "nsh: parse error: ... expected literal_span, ...".
`9foo = a` also works as assignment. `foo =` (nothing after `=`) is NOT an assignment:
runs command `foo`. `[ = a ]` does run `[` because `[` is not a valid variable name.
Inside double quotes nsh does NOT collapse backslashes: `echo "a\\b"` prints `a\\b` (two
backslashes). Tilde: `~` expands to HOME; `~user` prints warning `nsh: warning: ~user is
not yet supported` on stderr and expands to HOME anyway (user part ignored).

## echo

### Flag parsing rules (inferred)
- Only the FIRST argument is examined for flags. Later args are always literal.
- A flag arg must be exactly `-` followed by one or more DISTINCT letters from {n, e}.
  Valid: -n -e -ne -en. Invalid (treated as literal text): -E -N -x -nn -nne -enn - -- .
- `-n` suppresses the trailing newline. `-e` enables escape interpretation.
- With `-e`, ONLY `\n` (newline) and `\t` (tab) are interpreted. All other backslash
  sequences are literal, including: \\ \r \0 \x41 \c \a \b \v \f \z (backslash preserved).
- Args are joined with single spaces; a trailing newline is appended unless -n.
- Empty trailing args still get their separator: `echo x y ""` -> bytes `x y \n`.
- No args: prints just `\n`. `echo -n` alone: prints nothing.
- No option handling for `--` or `--help`/`--version` (printed literally).
- Exit code: always 0.

### Evidence

    echo -n hi                => out: "hi"  (no newline)         rc=0

## printf

printf is a faithful clone of **GNU coreutils 8.32 printf** (verified: builtin, works with
PATH=/nonexistent; `printf --version` prints `printf (GNU coreutils) 8.32` + FSF copyright;
`printf --help` prints the full GNU help text, rc=0).

### Rules
- Format string is reused cyclically until all args consumed: `printf "%s\n" a b c` -> `a\nb\nc\n`.
- No trailing newline added; `\n` in format is a real newline.
- If format contains NO conversions and extra args exist: warning on stderr
  `printf: warning: ignoring excess arguments, starting with 'ARG'` (rc still 0), format printed once.
  e.g. `printf "hi" a b` => out `hi`, err `printf: warning: ignoring excess arguments, starting with 'a'`, rc=0.
  `printf -v x "%s" hi` => out `-v`, same warning about 'x', rc=0 (no -v support).
- `printf -- FMT...`: `--` is consumed as end-of-options.
- Missing args: %d/%i -> 0, %f -> 0.000000, %s -> empty, %c -> NUL byte (\0), %b -> empty.
  `printf "%d|%s|%f|%c\n"` => bytes `0||0.000000|\0\n`, rc=0.
- Empty-string arg for %d: `printf "%d\n" ""` => `0\n`, rc=0, NO error.
- Conversions verified: %s %d %i %c %x %X %o %u %f %e %g %b %q %%.
  - %c takes first char of arg; empty arg -> NUL byte.
  - %u/%o/%x on negatives wrap as 64-bit: `printf "%u %o %x\n" -1 -5 -5` =>
    `18446744073709551615 1777777777777777777773 fffffffffffffffb`.
  - %f default precision 6 (`3.14159` -> `3.141590`); %e -> `3.141590e+04`; %g works.
  - %b interprets backslash escapes in the ARGUMENT (like echo -e of GNU): \t etc.; octal
    in %b args is `\0ooo` form; `\c` in %b arg stops ALL further output:
    `printf "%b" "a\cb"` => `a`, rc=0.
  - %q quotes for shell reuse: `printf "%q\n" "a b"` => `'a b'`; empty => `''`;
    `a'b` => `"a'b"`; safe strings printed bare (`hi` -> `hi`).
- Width/precision/flags all work: %5s %-5s %05d %-8d %+d `% d` %10.3s %.2f %5.1f %08.2f (`-3.14159` -> `-0003.14`).
- Integer args accept C-style constants and leading whitespace/sign: `" 42"`->42, `-7`->-7,
  `0x10`->16, `010`->8 (octal!), `'a`->97 (char constant).
- Escape sequences in FORMAT (GNU set): \" \\ \a \b \c \e \f \n \r \t \v,
  \NNN (1-3 octal digits, no leading 0), \0NNN (0-3 digits after \0), \xHH (1-2 hex digits),
  \uHHHH \UHHHHHHHH (per --help). Verified: `\1`,`\01`,`\001`->byte 1; `\0001`->`\0`+`1`;
  `\400`->`\0` (256 wraps mod 256); `\x4`->byte 4; `\x41`->`A`; `\041`->`!`; `\0101`->`\b`+`1`;
  `\c` in format stops output: `printf "a\cb"` => `a`.

## test and [

Same parser for both; `[` additionally requires a final `]` argument (stripped before parsing).
Error prefix is `test: ` or `[: ` accordingly. Exit codes: 0=true, 1=false, 2=error.
No --help/--version handling: `test --help` -> 0 (treated as non-empty string).

### Exit statuses / arity
    test                 => rc=1                [ ]              => rc=1
    test x               => rc=0                [ x ]            => rc=0
    test ""              => rc=1
    test -e              => rc=0  (single arg = non-empty-string test; applies to -z -n -a -o -t ! etc.)

### Unary file ops (all verified working; operand relative to cwd; symlinks followed except -L/-h)
-e -f -d -r -w -x -s (non-empty) -b -c -p -S -L -h -g -u -k -O -G -N -t FD

    test -f /tmp            => 1     test -d DIR => 0   test -f FILE => 0

    test -c /dev/null => 0  test -b /dev/null => 1

    test -t 0 => 1 (not a tty under -c)  test -t 9 => 1

    test abc == abc  => 0  (== supported)            test a == b => 1
    test abc != abd  => 0

### Integer ops (-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge); operands parsed as DECIMAL (leading whitespace,
### optional +/- allowed; leading zeros OK but still decimal: 01 -eq 1 true; NO hex/octal)
    test 1 -eq 1 => 0   test 01 -eq 1 => 0   test +5 -eq 5 => 0   test " 5" -eq 5 => 0
    test -1 -lt 0 => 0  ... all six ops behave normally

### File-to-file ops (GNU semantics)

    test /nonexistent -ef /nonexistent2 => 1

### Combinators and precedence
- `!` negates (binds tightest, repeatable): `test ! a = a` => 1; `test ! ! a = a` => 0;
  `test ! ! ! x` => 1.
- `-a` binds tighter than `-o`: `test a = a -o b = c -a c = d` => 0 (i.e. true || (false && false)).
  `test a = b -a c = c -o d = d` => 0 ((false && true) || true).
- Parentheses `\( \)` supported: `test \( a = a \)` => 0;
  `test ! \( -n x -a -z "" \)` => 1; nesting works.
- `test ! -n x -a -n y` => 1  (i.e. (!true) && true).

## true, false, :

- `:` is NOT a builtin: runs as external command lookup ->
  err: `nsh: command not found \`:'\n`, rc=1 (args ignored, same result).
- `true` (any args) => rc=0. `false` (any args) => rc=1.
- Both are GNU coreutils 8.32 clones: `true --help`/`false --help` print the GNU help text
  (rc 0 for true, 1 for false); `true --version` -> `true (GNU coreutils) 8.32\n` + copyright, rc=0;
  `false --version` prints same text with `false` name, rc=1.

## cd

- `cd` (no args) => chdir to HOME read from the PROCESS ENVIRONMENT (not shell variables!):
  `unset HOME; cd` still goes to the HOME the process inherited. rc=0.
- `cd ""` => silent no-op success (rc=0, cwd unchanged).
- `cd -` => go to PREVIOUSLY VISITED directory. NOT a simple OLDPWD swap: nsh keeps a
  history of visited directories; `cd -` walks BACKWARD through it and does not push a new
  entry. Evidence: cwd starts /workspace; `cd /tmp; cd /var; cd /usr; cd -` -> /var; `cd -` -> /tmp;
  `cd -` -> /workspace; further `cd -` => rc=1 (history exhausted, cwd unchanged, SILENT).
  A normal `cd X` after `cd -` pushes X onto the history; next `cd -` still resumes the
  backward walk (evidence: ...; cd - -> /var; cd /; cd - -> /var).
  `cd -` prints NOTHING (unlike bash). With no prior cd: rc=1, no output.
  The $OLDPWD/$PWD shell variables are IGNORED for this (setting OLDPWD=X; cd - does not use X).
- `cd` does NOT update $PWD or $OLDPWD variables (they keep inherited values).
- `cd ~` and `cd ~/sub` => tilde expands to HOME. `cd ~root` => stderr
  `nsh: warning: ~user is not yet supported\n`, then cds to HOME (user part dropped), rc=0.
- No flags: `cd -P dir` / `cd -L dir` treat `-P`/`-L` as the directory name (error below).
- Extra args silently ignored; only FIRST arg used: `cd a b c` tries to cd to `a`.
- CDPATH NOT supported: relative paths resolve only against cwd.
- Physical paths only: `cd /tmp/nshprobe/dlink` (symlink to d1); pwd => `/tmp/nshprobe/d1`.
  No logical PWD tracking anywhere.
- Error format (rc=1, stderr, Rust OS-error style; relative paths shown cwd-joined):
    cd /nonexistent_xyz   => `nsh: cd: No such file or directory (os error 2): \`/nonexistent_xyz'\n`
    cd a b c              => `nsh: cd: No such file or directory (os error 2): \`/workspace/a'\n`
    cd /tmp/nshprobe/file => `nsh: cd: Not a directory (os error 20): \`/tmp/nshprobe/file'\n`
    cd --help             => `nsh: cd: No such file or directory (os error 2): \`/workspace/--help'\n`
- Normalizations: `cd ..`, `cd .`, `cd a/../b` all behave per the OS (pwd shows resolved path).

## pwd

GNU coreutils 8.32 clone (builtin; works with PATH=/nonexistent).
- `pwd` => prints physical cwd + `\n`, rc=0. Always physical (no logical/symlink PWD).
- `-L` and `-P` both accepted and both print the PHYSICAL path (identical output);
  combined `-LP` fine. rc=0.
- `pwd --help` => GNU help text (`Usage: pwd [OPTION]...` ...), rc=0.
- `pwd --version` => `pwd (GNU coreutils) 8.32\n` + FSF copyright block, rc=0.
- Extra non-option args: prints cwd, rc=0, stderr: `pwd: ignoring non-option arguments\n`.
- Bad option: rc=1, no stdout, stderr:
  `pwd: invalid option -- 'x'\nTry 'pwd --help' for more information.\n`

## pushd / popd  (clap-v2-style CLI parsing; NOT bash semantics!)

- `pushd DIR`: pushes DIR onto the directory stack but DOES NOT chdir. Prints nothing.
  rc=0 even if DIR does not exist. `pushd` with no args: no-op, rc=0 (no swap!).
  `pushd +1`: silently accepted, no-op, rc=0. `pushd ""`: rc=0.
- `popd`: pops the TOP of stack and chdirs to it (cd-style). Prints nothing on success, rc=0.
  Evidence: `pushd d1; pushd d2; popd; pwd` => d2; another `popd; pwd` => d1.
  `cd d1; pushd d2; pwd` => d1 (pushd didn't move); `popd; pwd` => d2.
- `popd` on empty stack: rc=1, stderr: `nsh: popd: directory stack empty\n`.
- `popd` when popped dir invalid: rc=1, stderr cd-style:
  `nsh: popd: No such file or directory (os error 2): \`/nonexistent_xyz'\n`.
- `dirs` builtin does NOT exist: `nsh: command not found \`dirs'\n`, rc=1.
  There is no way to print the stack.
- Argument errors (rc=1, stderr, clap v2 style):
    pushd a b  /  pushd DIR extra =>
      `nsh: pushd: error: Found argument 'extra' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context\n\nUSAGE:\n    pushd [dir]\n\nFor more information try --help\n`
    popd extra / popd +1 =>
      `nsh: popd: error: Found argument 'extra' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context\n\nUSAGE:\n    popd\n\nFor more information try --help\n`
- `pushd --help` (also -h): rc=1, NOTHING on stdout, stderr exactly:
      nsh: pushd: pushd 0.4.2
      Pushd command.

      USAGE:
          pushd [dir]

      FLAGS:
          -h, --help       Prints help information
          -V, --version    Prints version information

      ARGS:
          <dir>    
  (note: 4 trailing spaces after `<dir>`, and a trailing blank line)
- `popd --help`: same shape, stderr:
      nsh: popd: popd 0.4.2
      Popd command.

      USAGE:
          popd

      FLAGS:
          -h, --help       Prints help information
          -V, --version    Prints version information
  (trailing blank line; rc=1)
- `pushd --version` / `popd --version`: stdout `pushd 0.4.2\n` (resp. `popd 0.4.2\n`),
  PLUS stderr `nsh: pushd: \n\n` (resp. popd), rc=1.

- echo: always 0.
- printf: 0 ok; 1 on any error (bad conversion, numeric conversion failure, missing operand);

- test/[: 0 true, 1 false, 2 usage/parse error.

- pwd: 0 ok (even with extra args), 1 on invalid option.

## echo

### Flag parsing rules (inferred)
- Only the FIRST argument is examined for flags. Later args are always literal.
- A flag arg must be exactly `-` followed by one or more DISTINCT letters from {n, e}.
  Valid: -n -e -ne -en. Invalid (treated as literal text): -E -N -x -nn -nne -enn - -- .
- `-n` suppresses the trailing newline. `-e` enables escape interpretation.
- With `-e`, ONLY `\n` (newline) and `\t` (tab) are interpreted. All other backslash
  sequences are literal, including: \\ \r \0 \x41 \c \a \b \v \f \z (backslash preserved).
- Args are joined with single spaces; a trailing newline is appended unless -n.
- Empty trailing args still get their separator: `echo x y ""` -> bytes `x y \n`.
- No args: prints just `\n`. `echo -n` alone: prints nothing.
- No option handling for `--` or `--help`/`--version` (printed literally).
- Exit code: always 0.

    echo -en "a\tb"     => bytes: `a TAB b` (no newline)         rc=0

## printf

printf is a faithful clone of **GNU coreutils 8.32 printf** (verified: builtin, works with
PATH=/nonexistent; `printf --version` prints `printf (GNU coreutils) 8.32` + FSF copyright;
`printf --help` prints the full GNU help text, rc=0).

### Rules
- Format string is reused cyclically until all args consumed: `printf "%s\n" a b c` -> `a\nb\nc\n`.
- No trailing newline added; `\n` in format is a real newline.
- If format contains NO conversions and extra args exist: warning on stderr
  `printf: warning: ignoring excess arguments, starting with 'ARG'` (rc still 0), format printed once.
  e.g. `printf "hi" a b` => out `hi`, err `printf: warning: ignoring excess arguments, starting with 'a'`, rc=0.
  `printf -v x "%s" hi` => out `-v`, same warning about 'x', rc=0 (no -v support).
- `printf -- FMT...`: `--` is consumed as end-of-options.
- Missing args: %d/%i -> 0, %f -> 0.000000, %s -> empty, %c -> NUL byte (\0), %b -> empty.
  `printf "%d|%s|%f|%c\n"` => bytes `0||0.000000|\0\n`, rc=0.
- Empty-string arg for %d: `printf "%d\n" ""` => `0\n`, rc=0, NO error.
- Conversions verified: %s %d %i %c %x %X %o %u %f %e %g %b %q %%.
  - %c takes first char of arg; empty arg -> NUL byte.
  - %u/%o/%x on negatives wrap as 64-bit: `printf "%u %o %x\n" -1 -5 -5` =>
    `18446744073709551615 1777777777777777777773 fffffffffffffffb`.
  - %f default precision 6 (`3.14159` -> `3.141590`); %e -> `3.141590e+04`; %g works.
  - %b interprets backslash escapes in the ARGUMENT (like echo -e of GNU): \t etc.; octal
    in %b args is `\0ooo` form; `\c` in %b arg stops ALL further output:
    `printf "%b" "a\cb"` => `a`, rc=0.
  - %q quotes for shell reuse: `printf "%q\n" "a b"` => `'a b'`; empty => `''`;
    `a'b` => `"a'b"`; safe strings printed bare (`hi` -> `hi`).
- Width/precision/flags all work: %5s %-5s %05d %-8d %+d `% d` %10.3s %.2f %5.1f %08.2f (`-3.14159` -> `-0003.14`).
- Integer args accept C-style constants and leading whitespace/sign: `" 42"`->42, `-7`->-7,
  `0x10`->16, `010`->8 (octal!), `'a`->97 (char constant).
- Escape sequences in FORMAT (GNU set): \" \\ \a \b \c \e \f \n \r \t \v,
  \NNN (1-3 octal digits, no leading 0), \0NNN (0-3 digits after \0), \xHH (1-2 hex digits),
  \uHHHH \UHHHHHHHH (per --help). Verified: `\1`,`\01`,`\001`->byte 1; `\0001`->`\0`+`1`;
  `\400`->`\0` (256 wraps mod 256); `\x4`->byte 4; `\x41`->`A`; `\041`->`!`; `\0101`->`\b`+`1`;
  `\c` in format stops output: `printf "a\cb"` => `a`.

### Error behavior (errors print to stderr, partial stdout kept, rc=1; script continues)
    printf                          => err: `printf: missing operand\nTry 'printf --help' for more information.\n`  rc=1
    printf "%d\n" abc               => out: `0\n`;  err: `printf: 'abc': expected a numeric value\n`               rc=1
    printf "%d\n" 12abc             => out: `12\n`; err: `printf: '12abc': value not completely converted\n`      rc=1
    printf "%d\n" 0x                => out: `0\n`;  err: `printf: '0x': value not completely converted\n`         rc=1
    printf "%d\n" 99999999999999999999999999
                                    => out: `9223372036854775807\n`;
                                       err: `printf: '99999999999999999999999999': Numerical result out of range\n` rc=1
    printf "%y\n" foo               => out: ``; err: `printf: %y: invalid conversion specification\n`             rc=1
    printf "a%yb\n" foo             => out: `a`; err: same as above (output stops at bad spec)                    rc=1
    printf "abc%"                   => out: `abc`; err: `printf: %: invalid conversion specification\n`           rc=1
    printf "%5%|\n"                 => out: ``; err: `printf: %5%: invalid conversion specification\n`            rc=1
    printf "\x4|\x|\n"              => out: byte(4)+`|`, err: `printf: missing hexadecimal number in escape\n`    rc=1
    (Note: bad-arg errors like 'abc' still PRINT the converted value 0 and continue the format;
     invalid-conversion errors stop output at the offending spec.)
