args.command:
cat > /workspace/specs/builtins_io.md <<'SPECEOF'
# nsh 0.4.2 — IO/process builtins spec (source, exec, eval, read, wait, jobs, fg, bg, kill, break, continue)

Method: black-box probing of `/workspace/executable` (nsh 0.4.2) via `--norc -c '...'` with isolated
HOME, capturing stdout/stderr separately. All tests were run non-interactively (`-c`); interactive
behavior may differ (noted where relevant). Nondeterministic values (PIDs, backtrace addresses)
are marked [ND].

General conventions observed:
- Builtin errors print to stderr; the script usually CONTINUES after a builtin error.
- `$?` after a builtin error is usually 1; the overall exit code of `-c` is the exit status of the
  last command executed (0 if the last command succeeded), unless the shell panics (101) or hits
  a top-level parse error (255).
- `$?` can be `-1` after a parse error inside `eval`/`source` (see below).

================================================================================
## source  (`.` is NOT a synonym)
================================================================================

### source runs file in current shell; variables persist
Input:  /tmp/src1.sh contains: echo INSIDE\nx=42
  ./executable --norc -c 'source /tmp/src1.sh; echo "x=$x"'
stdout: "INSIDE\nx=42\n"   stderr: empty   exit=0

### source of nonexistent file: error on stderr, script continues, status 1
  ./executable --norc -c 'source /tmp/nonexistent.sh; echo after'
stdout: "after\n"
stderr: nsh: failed open the file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }
exit=0  ($? of the source command itself is 1)

### source of a directory
stderr: nsh: failed open the file: Os { code: 21, kind: IsADirectory, message: "Is a directory" }
$?=1, script continues, overall exit=0.

### source with no args
  ./executable --norc -c 'source; echo "status=$?"'
stderr: nsh: source: filename argument required
stdout: "status=0\n"   exit=0        <-- NOTE: status is 0 despite the error message!

### No PATH search: bare filename resolved against CWD only
  PATH=/dir/containing/mylib.sh:$PATH; source mylib.sh
  -> same NotFound Os{...} error as above unless CWD contains the file.
  `source src2.sh` works when CWD contains src2.sh.

### Arguments to source are silently ignored (NOT set as $1, $2, ...)
  /tmp/src2.sh: echo "arg1=$1 arg2=$2"
  ./executable --norc -c 'source /tmp/src2.sh aa bb'   -> stdout "arg1= arg2=\n"
  ($0 is also empty in -c mode regardless.)

### source exit status = status of last command in the file
  file containing `false`:  source f.sh; echo $?  -> 1
  If source is the last command of -c, the shell exit code equals it (exit=1 for `false`).

### `exit N` inside sourced file exits the whole shell immediately with code N
  file: echo before; exit 3; echo never
  -> stdout "before\n", exit=3, nothing after source runs.

### `return` inside sourced file -> PANIC (see "Panics" section)
  file: echo b4; return 7; echo never
  stdout: "b4\n"
  stderr starts: "nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:133:14:\nunexpected Return\n" + backtrace [ND]
  exit=101

### syntax error inside sourced file: NOTHING in the file executes; shell continues; $? = -1
  file: echo BEFORE / if if / echo AFTER
  ./executable --norc -c 'source /tmp/badsyn.sh; echo "s=$?"'
  stdout: "s=-1\n"   exit=0
  stderr: parse error pointing at line AFTER the file's last line (here line 4, col 1):
    nsh: parse error:  --> 4:1
      |
    4 | 
      | ^---
      |
      = expected normal_newline, command, or compound_list_sep

### `.` is not source
  ./executable --norc -c '. /tmp/src1.sh'
  stderr: nsh: command not found `.'     ($?=1, script continues, exit=0)

================================================================================
## exec
================================================================================

### exec CMD replaces the shell (external commands only, PATH lookup)
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec echo hi; echo after'
  stdout: "hi\n"  exit=0  ("after" never runs; uses execvp, so /bin/echo)
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec sh -c "echo fromsh"'   -> stdout "fromsh\n" exit=0
  Multi-arg: exec printf "a=%s b=%s\n" 1 2  -> "a=1 b=2\n", exit=0.

### exec nonexistent: shell does NOT exit; error; status 127; script continues
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec /nonexistent_cmd_xyz; echo "status=$?"'
  stderr: nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory
  stdout: "status=127\n"   exit=0
  Builtin names fail too (not looked up as builtins): `exec cd /` ->
  stderr "nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory", then `after` runs.
  `exec /tmp` (directory): stderr "nsh: exec: EACCES: Permission denied", status 126, continues.

### REDIRECTIONS ON exec ARE IGNORED (but the file is still created/truncated)
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec >/tmp/execredir.txt; echo x'
  -> stdout "x\n"; /tmp/execredir.txt exists but is EMPTY; exit=0.
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec echo hi >/tmp/er.txt; echo after'
  -> stdout "hi\n"; file empty. (redirect ignored, then exec replaced shell; "after" never ran)

### exec with no args: no-op, status 0
  `exec; echo after` -> "after\n", exit=0.

================================================================================
## eval
================================================================================

### basic
  eval "echo hi"            -> "hi\n", exit=0
  eval "echo a; echo b"     -> "a\nb\n"  (full script parsing)
  eval (no args)            -> no-op, status 0
  eval "  " (whitespace)    -> no-op, status 0
  eval "false"              -> status 1
  eval of last command propagates to shell exit as usual.

### Multiple args are joined with single spaces, then evaluated
  eval echo hello world     -> "hello world\n"
  eval echo "a  b"          -> "a b\n"  (arg splitting collapses: eval receives "echo" "a  b",
                              joined as "echo a  b", re-parsed -> two words)

### Assignments persist in current shell
  eval "y=99"; echo $y      -> 99

### eval of `exit N` exits the shell with N.
### eval of `return` -> PANIC "unexpected Return" (exit 101), same as source.

### eval'd break/continue propagate into enclosing loops correctly
  for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; eval "break"; done; echo after   -> "1\nafter\n", exit=0

### REDIRECTIONS ON eval ARE IGNORED (file created/truncated but output not redirected)
  eval "echo hi" >/tmp/ev.txt  -> "hi\n" on stdout, file empty.

### Parse error inside eval: message printed, script continues, $? = -1
  ./executable --norc -c 'eval "if if"; echo "status=$?"'
  stdout: "status=-1\n"   exit=0
  stderr:
    nsh: parse error:  --> 1:7
      |
    1 | if if 
      |       ^---
      |
      = expected command or compound_list_sep
  If the eval is the LAST command of -c, overall exit=255 (the -1 becomes 255).

================================================================================
## read
================================================================================

read accepts EXACTLY ONE variable name. There is no word splitting, no REPLY default,
no multi-var support. IFS is ignored. Leading/trailing whitespace is PRESERVED.
The line's trailing newline is stripped; a trailing \r before the newline is also stripped.

### basic
  echo 'hello world' | nsh -c 'read v; echo "<$v>"'        -> "<hello world>\n", exit=0, read status 0
  printf '  hi there  \n' | ... 'read v; echo "<$v>"'      -> "<  hi there  >\n" (whitespace kept)
  printf 'a\r\n' | ...                                     -> "<a>\n"  (\r stripped)
  echo 'a:b:c' | ... 'IFS=:; read v; echo "<$v>"'          -> "<a:b:c>\n" (IFS ignored)
  Backslashes are always literal (no -r needed):
  printf 'a\\tb\\c\n' | ... 'read v; echo "<$v>"'          -> "<a\tb\c>\n"

### EOF behavior
  empty stdin:   read v -> status 1, v set to "" (v=<>) ; script continues
  /dev/null:     read v </dev/null -> status 1
  partial last line without newline: printf 'nonl' | read v -> status 0, v="nonl"

### read from redirect / pipeline
  read v < file                      -> works (v = first line)
  echo abc | read v; echo $v         -> "abc"  (LAST pipeline element runs in CURRENT shell!)
  Multiple reads share stdin: printf 'l1\nl2\n' | 'read a; read b' -> a=l1 b=l2

### -p PROMPT: accepted, but the prompt is NEVER displayed (not on stdout, stderr, or even a pty)
  echo val | nsh -c 'read -p "Enter: " v; echo "<$v>"'   -> "<val>\n", nothing else, exit=0

### -r, -s, -n, -t are NOT supported -> clap-style error, status 1, script continues:
  read -r v:
    stderr:
      read: error: Found argument '-r' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

      USAGE:
          read [OPTIONS] <VAR>

      For more information try --help
    (v ends up empty; same text with '-s', '-n', '2' etc. substituted)

### no args -> clap error, status 1:
    read: error: The following required arguments were not provided:
        <VAR>

    USAGE:
        read [OPTIONS] <VAR>

    For more information try --help
  (`read -p` without VAR: same but USAGE line is "    read <VAR> -p <prompt>")

### extra positional -> clap error, status 1:
    read: error: Found argument 'b' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context
    ... (same USAGE block)

### read --help -> prints help to STDERR, exit code 1 (and -c overall exit=1):
    read: read 0.4.2
    read command.

    USAGE:
        read [OPTIONS] <VAR>

    FLAGS:
        -h, --help       Prints help information
        -V, --version    Prints version information

    OPTIONS:
        -p <prompt>        

    ARGS:
        <VAR>    

### read --version -> stdout: "read 0.4.2" (NO trailing newline); stderr: "read: \n\n"; exit=1.

### Any string is accepted as the variable name (e.g. read "a=b" succeeds, status 0).

================================================================================
## Job control model (NON-INTERACTIVE; crucial)
================================================================================

In `-c` mode the shell effectively serializes background jobs:
- `cmd &` spawns the job, but BEFORE the next command is executed the shell performs a
  BLOCKING reap of all spawned children and prints a completion notification for each.
  Proof: `time nsh -c 'sleep 1 & echo fast'` -> real 1.01s; output:
      [1] Done: sleep 1
      fast
  Two jobs run sequentially: `sleep 1 & sleep 1 & echo done` takes ~2.01s.
- The shell also blocks-reaps at end of script: `sleep 2 &` alone takes ~2.0s and prints
      [1] Done: sleep 2
  before exiting (exit=0).

### Notification format (to the shell's OWN stdout; NOT affected by the next command's redirects):
    [1] Done: <original source text of the command>
- Job id is ALWAYS 1 (even for multiple jobs: three concurrent jobs print three "[1] Done:" lines).
- Status is ALWAYS "Done:" — exit status and signals are NOT reflected:
    false &                       -> "[1] Done: false"
    sh -c 'kill -KILL $$' &       -> "[1] Done: sh -c \"kill -KILL \$\$\"" (raw source text shown)
- Pipelines: `sleep 0.1 | cat &` -> "[1] Done: sleep 0.1 | cat"
- NO notification / job entry is created for:
  * builtins in background: `echo hi & true; echo after` -> "hi\nafter\n" (no Done line)
  * variable assignments: `x=5 & true; echo $x` -> "5" (assignment applies to current shell!)
  * compound commands: `if true; then sleep 2; fi & echo quick` -> waits 2s, prints only "quick"
  * subshells: `(sleep 2) & echo quick` -> waits 2s, prints only "quick"
- `$!` is set to the bg job's PID [ND]; `$!` is `0` when no job has been started.

================================================================================
## jobs
================================================================================

### jobs lists current jobs; because of the blocking reap, entries are always "Done":
  sleep 2 & jobs   -> "[1] Done: sleep 2\n" on stdout, exit=0 (yes: it waited 2s first)
  jobs with no jobs -> no output, status 0.

### jobs takes NO arguments (clap error, status 1, script continues).
  NOTE THE BUG: error messages use the binary name "fg" instead of "jobs":
  `jobs -l` or `jobs foo`:
    stderr:
      fg: error: Found argument '-l' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

      USAGE:
          jobs

      For more information try --help
### jobs --help -> STDERR, exit 1:
      fg: jobs 0.4.2
      jobs command.

      USAGE:
          jobs

      FLAGS:
          -h, --help       Prints help information
          -V, --version    Prints version information
### jobs --version -> stdout "jobs 0.4.2" (no newline), stderr "fg: \n\n", exit 1.

================================================================================
## wait
================================================================================

### wait (no args): waits for all jobs (already reaped anyway); ALWAYS status 0 —
  exit status of jobs is NOT propagated:
    sh -c "exit 7" & wait; echo $?    -> 0   (with "[1] Done: sh -c \"exit 7\"" on stdout first)
    wait with no jobs at all          -> status 0, no output.

### wait %N: job spec parsed (leading % stripped), but by the time wait runs the job is
  already reaped and removed, so it always fails:
    sleep 0.1 & wait %1    -> stdout "[1] Done: sleep 0.1\n", stderr "nsh: no such job \`1'", status 1
    wait %99 (never existed) -> stderr "nsh: no such job \`99'", status 1

### wait with anything not starting with %:
    wait 1     -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`1'", status 1
    wait xyz   -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`xyz'", status 1
    wait PID   -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`PID'" (PIDs are NOT accepted), status 1

### wait --help -> STDERR, exit 1:
      wait: wait 0.4.2
      wait command.

      USAGE:
          wait [job_id]

      FLAGS:
          -h, --help       Prints help information
          -V, --version    Prints version information

      ARGS:
          <job_id>    

================================================================================
## fg / bg
================================================================================

### With no jobs:
  fg; echo $?  -> stderr "nsh: no jobs to run", status 1
  bg; echo $?  -> stderr "nsh: no jobs to run", status 1
  (Even right after `sleep 0.1 &`, the job is already reaped, so fg/bg always see "no jobs".)

### With a job spec:
  fg %1 / bg %1   -> stderr "nsh: no such job \`1'", status 1
  fg %2           -> stderr "nsh: no such job \`2'", status 1
  fg 1            -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`1'", status 1   (no % = invalid)
  fg %%           -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`%'", status 1   (only one % stripped)
  fg xyz          -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`xyz'", status 1

### fg --help -> STDERR, exit 1:
      nsh: fg: fg 0.4.2
      fg command.

      USAGE:
          fg [job_id]

      FLAGS:
          -h, --help       Prints help information
          -V, --version    Prints version information

      ARGS:
          <job_id>    
### bg --help: same shape but first line is "bg: bg 0.4.2" and "bg command."/"bg [job_id]".

================================================================================
## kill
================================================================================

IMPORTANT ENVIRONMENT NOTE: every observed message of the kill builtin is byte-identical to
this system's /bin/kill (procps-ng 3.3.17), including usage text and quirks. It appears the
builtin delegates to (or exactly clones) procps kill. Reimplementation should reproduce these
strings; they may vary with the host's procps version.

### kill PID (numeric only; job specs NOT supported)
  kill <live-pid>        -> sends SIGTERM, status 0
  kill <pid> <pid2> ...  -> multiple PIDs OK, status 0
  kill 12345 (no such)   -> stderr "kill: (12345): No such process", status 1

================================================================================
## break / continue
================================================================================

### They take NO arguments. `break 2`, `break foo`, `continue 2` are PARSE ERRORS (exit 255):
  ./executable --norc -c 'for i in 1 2; do break 2; done'
    stderr:
      nsh: parse error:  --> 1:24
        |
      1 | for i in 1 2; do break 2; done
        |                        ^---
        |
        = expected and_or_list_sep or compound_list_sep

### In `for` loops they work correctly (directly, inside if, inside case, via eval):
  for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; break; done; echo after        -> 1, after
  for i in 1 2 3; do continue; echo $i; done; echo after     -> after
  for i in 1 2 3 4; do if test $i -eq 2; then continue; fi; echo $i; done  -> 1 3 4
  for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do if test $i -eq 3; then break; fi; echo $i; done   -> 1 2
  for i in 1 2 3; do case $i in 2) break;; *) echo $i;; esac; done; echo after -> 1, after
  Nested for: break exits only the inner for:
    for i in 1 2 3; do for j in a b c; do echo "$i$j"; break; done; done   -> 1a 2a 3a

### In `while` loops they are BROKEN (this is the surprising part). Model that fits all
  observations: break/continue abort the current command-list evaluation and set a pending
  control-flow signal. `for` consumes it (break=stop, continue=next iteration). `while`
  IGNORES it for loop control — it re-evaluates the condition and keeps looping — and if the
  LAST body execution ended with the signal pending, the signal becomes the while's own result
  and propagates outward.

  Observed cases:
  a) break directly in while body:
       i=0; while test $i -lt 5; do i=$((i+1)); echo $i; break; done; echo after
     -> prints 1 2 3 4 5 (loop NOT broken!), "after" never prints, then PANIC:
        "unexpected Break", exit=101.
  b) continue directly in while body:
       i=0; while test $i -lt 3; do i=$((i+1)); continue; echo $i; done; echo after
     -> prints nothing (body aborted each iteration), then PANIC "unexpected Continue", exit=101.
  c) break inside if inside while:
       ... if test $i -eq 2; then break; echo X; fi; echo "end$i"; done; echo after
     -> at i=2 the rest of the iteration is skipped (acts like continue), loop CONTINUES to
        completion, NO panic, exit=0 (prints iter1,end1,iter2,iter3,end3,after).
  d) continue inside if inside while -> works as a proper continue (1 3 4 after, exit=0).
  e) Pending signal propagates out of while and is consumed by an enclosing for:
       for x in X Y; do i=0; while test $i -lt 2; do i=$((i+1)); echo "$x$i"; break; done;
         echo "innerdone$x"; done; echo after
     -> X1 X2 after   (pending Break aborts for body — "innerdone" skipped — and stops the for)
       same with continue:
     -> X1 X2 Y1 Y2 after   (pending Continue skips rest of for body, for goes on)

### Outside any loop -> PANIC:
  break; echo after     -> stdout empty, exit=101, stderr:
      nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:133:14:
      unexpected Break
      [backtrace, ND]
      nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues
  continue; echo after  -> identical but "unexpected Continue".

### `until` does not exist (parse error), so only for/while matter.

================================================================================
## Panics (shared format)
================================================================================

Triggered by: `return` at top level (also inside source/eval), `break`/`continue` outside a
loop or left pending after a `while` loop.
- stderr first two lines (deterministic):
    nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:133:14:
    unexpected Break            (or: unexpected Continue / unexpected Return)
- then a Rust backtrace with [ND] addresses, then final line:
    nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues
- exit code 101.
- The panic is also appended (ANSI-colored) to ~/.nsh.log.

================================================================================
## CONDENSED RULES
================================================================================

source FILE:
  1. `.` is NOT an alias ("command not found `.'"). No PATH search; relative to CWD.
  2. Runs in current shell; assignments persist; args ignored (not bound to $1...).
  3. Missing file: stderr "nsh: failed open the file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: \"No such file or directory\" }", status 1, continue. Directory: code 21 IsADirectory variant.
  4. No args: "nsh: source: filename argument required", but status 0.
  5. Status = last command's status; `exit N` exits shell with N; `return` panics (101);
     syntax error -> nothing executes, status -1, shell continues.

exec [CMD ARGS...]:
  1. execvp only (no builtins). Success: replaces shell. Failure: "nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory" (status 127) or "nsh: exec: EACCES: Permission denied" (126); shell continues.
  2. No args: no-op, status 0.
  3. Redirections on exec/eval are silently ignored (target file still created/truncated).

eval [ARGS...]:
  1. Args joined with single spaces and re-parsed/executed in current shell.
  2. No args/whitespace: status 0. Status = last command. Parse error inside: message printed,
     status -1, shell continues (overall exit 255 if it was the last command).
  3. exit/return/break/continue inside eval behave as if written inline.

read [-p PROMPT] VAR:
  1. Exactly one VAR. No splitting, no REPLY, IFS ignored, whitespace preserved,
     trailing \n (and \r\n) stripped, backslashes literal.
  2. Status 0 on a line read (incl. unterminated final line); status 1 at EOF (VAR set to "").
  3. -p accepted, prompt never displayed. -r/-s/-n/-t/extra args: clap error on stderr
     ("read: error: Found argument 'X' ..."), status 1, script continues.
  4. Missing VAR: "read: error: The following required arguments were not provided:\n    <VAR>\n\nUSAGE:\n    read [OPTIONS] <VAR>\n\nFor more information try --help", status 1.
  5. --help: help to stderr, exit 1. --version: stdout "read 0.4.2" w/o newline + stderr "read: \n\n", exit 1.
  6. As last pipeline element, runs in the CURRENT shell.

Background / jobs:
  1. Before executing each new command (and before exiting), the shell blocking-waits for all
     bg children and prints "[1] Done: <source text>" to its own stdout for each TRACKED job.
  2. Tracked = external simple commands and pipelines. Builtins, assignments, compound
     commands and subshells run untracked (no notification, no jobs entry) but still block
     the next command.
  3. Job id is always 1; notification always says "Done:" regardless of exit status/signal.
  4. $! = last bg PID ("0" if none).
  5. jobs: prints "[N] Done: ..." lines (always Done non-interactively); any argument ->
     clap error under the wrong name "fg" ("fg: error: Found argument ..."), status 1.
  6. wait: no args -> status 0 always (exit statuses not propagated). "%N" -> "nsh: no such job \`N'";
     anything else -> "nsh: invalid job id \`X'"; status 1.
  7. fg/bg: no jobs -> "nsh: no jobs to run" (status 1); "%N" -> "nsh: no such job \`N'";
     other -> "nsh: invalid job id \`X'".
  8. --help of jobs/fg/bg/wait prints clap help to STDERR, exit 1 (jobs help header is the
     buggy "fg: jobs 0.4.2"; fg's is "nsh: fg: fg 0.4.2").

kill:
  1. Numeric PIDs only: kill [-SIG] PID...; % specs and junk ->
     "kill: failed to parse argument: 'X'" (status 1); dead PID ->
     "kill: (PID): No such process" (status 1); success status 0.
  2. -l (list, exit 0), "-l N" (name), -L (table), --help (stdout, exit 0),
     --version ("kill from procps-ng 3.3.17"). No args or bad signal -> usage on stderr,
     status 1. All text identical to procps-ng 3.3.17 /bin/kill.

break/continue:
  1. No arguments allowed (parse error, exit 255).
  2. Work correctly in `for` (incl. inside if/case/eval); innermost for only.
  3. In `while`: ignored for loop control; they abort the current body command list; if the
     signal is still pending after the while's final iteration, it propagates outward —
     consumed by an enclosing for, or PANIC ("unexpected Break"/"unexpected Continue", 101)
     at top level. break-in-if inside while degrades to a continue-like skip, no panic.
  4. Outside loops: panic main.rs:133, exit 101.

Method: black-box probing of `/workspace/executable` (nsh 0.4.2) via `--norc -c '...'` with isolated

## source  (`.` is NOT a synonym)
================================================================================

### source runs file in current shell; variables persist
Input:  /tmp/src1.sh contains: echo INSIDE\nx=42
  ./executable --norc -c 'source /tmp/src1.sh; echo "x=$x"'
stdout: "INSIDE\nx=42\n"   stderr: empty   exit=0

### source of nonexistent file: error on stderr, script continues, status 1
  ./executable --norc -c 'source /tmp/nonexistent.sh; echo after'
stdout: "after\n"
stderr: nsh: failed open the file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }
exit=0  ($? of the source command itself is 1)

### source of a directory
stderr: nsh: failed open the file: Os { code: 21, kind: IsADirectory, message: "Is a directory" }
$?=1, script continues, overall exit=0.

### source with no args
  ./executable --norc -c 'source; echo "status=$?"'
stderr: nsh: source: filename argument required
stdout: "status=0\n"   exit=0        <-- NOTE: status is 0 despite the error message!

  PATH=/dir/containing/mylib.sh:$PATH; source mylib.sh

  ($0 is also empty in -c mode regardless.)

### source exit status = status of last command in the file
  file containing `false`:  source f.sh; echo $?  -> 1
  If source is the last command of -c, the shell exit code equals it (exit=1 for `false`).

### `exit N` inside sourced file exits the whole shell immediately with code N
  file: echo before; exit 3; echo never
  -> stdout "before\n", exit=3, nothing after source runs.

### `return` inside sourced file -> PANIC (see "Panics" section)
  file: echo b4; return 7; echo never
  stdout: "b4\n"
  stderr starts: "nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:133:14:\nunexpected Return\n" + backtrace [ND]
  exit=101

### syntax error inside sourced file: NOTHING in the file executes; shell continues; $? = -1
  file: echo BEFORE / if if / echo AFTER
  ./executable --norc -c 'source /tmp/badsyn.sh; echo "s=$?"'
  stdout: "s=-1\n"   exit=0
  stderr: parse error pointing at line AFTER the file's last line (here line 4, col 1):

      |
    4 | 
      | ^---
      |

================================================================================
## exec
================================================================================

### exec CMD replaces the shell (external commands only, PATH lookup)
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec echo hi; echo after'
  stdout: "hi\n"  exit=0  ("after" never runs; uses execvp, so /bin/echo)
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec sh -c "echo fromsh"'   -> stdout "fromsh\n" exit=0
  Multi-arg: exec printf "a=%s b=%s\n" 1 2  -> "a=1 b=2\n", exit=0.

### exec nonexistent: shell does NOT exit; error; status 127; script continues
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec /nonexistent_cmd_xyz; echo "status=$?"'
  stderr: nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory
  stdout: "status=127\n"   exit=0
  Builtin names fail too (not looked up as builtins): `exec cd /` ->
  stderr "nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory", then `after` runs.
  `exec /tmp` (directory): stderr "nsh: exec: EACCES: Permission denied", status 126, continues.

### REDIRECTIONS ON exec ARE IGNORED (but the file is still created/truncated)
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec >/tmp/execredir.txt; echo x'
  -> stdout "x\n"; /tmp/execredir.txt exists but is EMPTY; exit=0.
  ./executable --norc -c 'exec echo hi >/tmp/er.txt; echo after'
  -> stdout "hi\n"; file empty. (redirect ignored, then exec replaced shell; "after" never ran)

### exec with no args: no-op, status 0
  `exec; echo after` -> "after\n", exit=0.

## eval
================================================================================

### basic
  eval "echo hi"            -> "hi\n", exit=0
  eval "echo a; echo b"     -> "a\nb\n"  (full script parsing)
  eval (no args)            -> no-op, status 0
  eval "  " (whitespace)    -> no-op, status 0
  eval "false"              -> status 1
  eval of last command propagates to shell exit as usual.

### Multiple args are joined with single spaces, then evaluated
  eval echo hello world     -> "hello world\n"
  eval echo "a  b"          -> "a b\n"  (arg splitting collapses: eval receives "echo" "a  b",
                              joined as "echo a  b", re-parsed -> two words)

### Assignments persist in current shell
  eval "y=99"; echo $y      -> 99

### eval of `exit N` exits the shell with N.
### eval of `return` -> PANIC "unexpected Return" (exit 101), same as source.

### eval'd break/continue propagate into enclosing loops correctly
  for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; eval "break"; done; echo after   -> "1\nafter\n", exit=0

### REDIRECTIONS ON eval ARE IGNORED (file created/truncated but output not redirected)
  eval "echo hi" >/tmp/ev.txt  -> "hi\n" on stdout, file empty.

### Parse error inside eval: message printed, script continues, $? = -1
  ./executable --norc -c 'eval "if if"; echo "status=$?"'
  stdout: "status=-1\n"   exit=0
  stderr:
    nsh: parse error:  --> 1:7
      |
    1 | if if 
      |       ^---
      |
      = expected command or compound_list_sep
  If the eval is the LAST command of -c, overall exit=255 (the -1 becomes 255).

================================================================================
## read
================================================================================

read accepts EXACTLY ONE variable name. There is no word splitting, no REPLY default,
no multi-var support. IFS is ignored. Leading/trailing whitespace is PRESERVED.
The line's trailing newline is stripped; a trailing \r before the newline is also stripped.

### basic
  echo 'hello world' | nsh -c 'read v; echo "<$v>"'        -> "<hello world>\n", exit=0, read status 0
  printf '  hi there  \n' | ... 'read v; echo "<$v>"'      -> "<  hi there  >\n" (whitespace kept)
  printf 'a\r\n' | ...                                     -> "<a>\n"  (\r stripped)
  echo 'a:b:c' | ... 'IFS=:; read v; echo "<$v>"'          -> "<a:b:c>\n" (IFS ignored)
  Backslashes are always literal (no -r needed):
  printf 'a\\tb\\c\n' | ... 'read v; echo "<$v>"'          -> "<a\tb\c>\n"

### EOF behavior
  empty stdin:   read v -> status 1, v set to "" (v=<>) ; script continues
  /dev/null:     read v </dev/null -> status 1
  partial last line without newline: printf 'nonl' | read v -> status 0, v="nonl"

### read from redirect / pipeline
  read v < file                      -> works (v = first line)
  echo abc | read v; echo $v         -> "abc"  (LAST pipeline element runs in CURRENT shell!)
  Multiple reads share stdin: printf 'l1\nl2\n' | 'read a; read b' -> a=l1 b=l2

### -p PROMPT: accepted, but the prompt is NEVER displayed (not on stdout, stderr, or even a pty)
  echo val | nsh -c 'read -p "Enter: " v; echo "<$v>"'   -> "<val>\n", nothing else, exit=0

### -r, -s, -n, -t are NOT supported -> clap-style error, status 1, script continues:
  read -r v:
    stderr:
      read: error: Found argument '-r' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

      USAGE:
          read [OPTIONS] <VAR>

      For more information try --help
    (v ends up empty; same text with '-s', '-n', '2' etc. substituted)

### no args -> clap error, status 1:
    read: error: The following required arguments were not provided:
        <VAR>

    USAGE:
        read [OPTIONS] <VAR>

    For more information try --help
  (`read -p` without VAR: same but USAGE line is "    read <VAR> -p <prompt>")

### extra positional -> clap error, status 1:
    read: error: Found argument 'b' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context
    ... (same USAGE block)

### read --help -> prints help to STDERR, exit code 1 (and -c overall exit=1):
    read: read 0.4.2
    read command.

    USAGE:
        read [OPTIONS] <VAR>

    FLAGS:
        -h, --help       Prints help information
        -V, --version    Prints version information

    OPTIONS:
        -p <prompt>        

    ARGS:
        <VAR>    

### read --version -> stdout: "read 0.4.2" (NO trailing newline); stderr: "read: \n\n"; exit=1.

### Any string is accepted as the variable name (e.g. read "a=b" succeeds, status 0).

================================================================================
## Job control model (NON-INTERACTIVE; crucial)
================================================================================

In `-c` mode the shell effectively serializes background jobs:
- `cmd &` spawns the job, but BEFORE the next command is executed the shell performs a
  BLOCKING reap of all spawned children and prints a completion notification for each.
  Proof: `time nsh -c 'sleep 1 & echo fast'` -> real 1.01s; output:
      [1] Done: sleep 1
      fast
  Two jobs run sequentially: `sleep 1 & sleep 1 & echo done` takes ~2.01s.
- The shell also blocks-reaps at end of script: `sleep 2 &` alone takes ~2.0s and prints
      [1] Done: sleep 2
  before exiting (exit=0).

### Notification format (to the shell's OWN stdout; NOT affected by the next command's redirects):
    [1] Done: <original source text of the command>
- Job id is ALWAYS 1 (even for multiple jobs: three concurrent jobs print three "[1] Done:" lines).
- Status is ALWAYS "Done:" — exit status and signals are NOT reflected:
    false &                       -> "[1] Done: false"
    sh -c 'kill -KILL $$' &       -> "[1] Done: sh -c \"kill -KILL \$\$\"" (raw source text shown)
- Pipelines: `sleep 0.1 | cat &` -> "[1] Done: sleep 0.1 | cat"
- NO notification / job entry is created for:
  * builtins in background: `echo hi & true; echo after` -> "hi\nafter\n" (no Done line)
  * variable assignments: `x=5 & true; echo $x` -> "5" (assignment applies to current shell!)
  * compound commands: `if true; then sleep 2; fi & echo quick` -> waits 2s, prints only "quick"
  * subshells: `(sleep 2) & echo quick` -> waits 2s, prints only "quick"
- `$!` is set to the bg job's PID [ND]; `$!` is `0` when no job has been started.

## jobs
================================================================================

### jobs lists current jobs; because of the blocking reap, entries are always "Done":
  sleep 2 & jobs   -> "[1] Done: sleep 2\n" on stdout, exit=0 (yes: it waited 2s first)
  jobs with no jobs -> no output, status 0.

### jobs takes NO arguments (clap error, status 1, script continues).
  NOTE THE BUG: error messages use the binary name "fg" instead of "jobs":
  `jobs -l` or `jobs foo`:
    stderr:
      fg: error: Found argument '-l' which wasn't expected, or isn't valid in this context

      USAGE:
          jobs

      For more information try --help
### jobs --help -> STDERR, exit 1:
      fg: jobs 0.4.2
      jobs command.

      USAGE:
          jobs

      FLAGS:
          -h, --help       Prints help information
          -V, --version    Prints version information
### jobs --version -> stdout "jobs 0.4.2" (no newline), stderr "fg: \n\n", exit 1.

## wait
================================================================================

### wait (no args): waits for all jobs (already reaped anyway); ALWAYS status 0 —
  exit status of jobs is NOT propagated:
    sh -c "exit 7" & wait; echo $?    -> 0   (with "[1] Done: sh -c \"exit 7\"" on stdout first)
    wait with no jobs at all          -> status 0, no output.

### wait %N: job spec parsed (leading % stripped), but by the time wait runs the job is
  already reaped and removed, so it always fails:
    sleep 0.1 & wait %1    -> stdout "[1] Done: sleep 0.1\n", stderr "nsh: no such job \`1'", status 1
    wait %99 (never existed) -> stderr "nsh: no such job \`99'", status 1

### wait with anything not starting with %:
    wait 1     -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`1'", status 1
    wait xyz   -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`xyz'", status 1
    wait PID   -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`PID'" (PIDs are NOT accepted), status 1

### wait --help -> STDERR, exit 1:
      wait: wait 0.4.2
      wait command.

      USAGE:
          wait [job_id]

      FLAGS:
          -h, --help       Prints help information
          -V, --version    Prints version information

      ARGS:
          <job_id>

## fg / bg
================================================================================

### With no jobs:
  fg; echo $?  -> stderr "nsh: no jobs to run", status 1
  bg; echo $?  -> stderr "nsh: no jobs to run", status 1
  (Even right after `sleep 0.1 &`, the job is already reaped, so fg/bg always see "no jobs".)

### With a job spec:
  fg %1 / bg %1   -> stderr "nsh: no such job \`1'", status 1
  fg %2           -> stderr "nsh: no such job \`2'", status 1
  fg 1            -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`1'", status 1   (no % = invalid)
  fg %%           -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`%'", status 1   (only one % stripped)
  fg xyz          -> stderr "nsh: invalid job id \`xyz'", status 1

### fg --help -> STDERR, exit 1:
      nsh: fg: fg 0.4.2
      fg command.

      USAGE:
          fg [job_id]

      FLAGS:
          -h, --help       Prints help information
          -V, --version    Prints version information

      ARGS:
          <job_id>

## kill
================================================================================

IMPORTANT ENVIRONMENT NOTE: every observed message of the kill builtin is byte-identical to
this system's /bin/kill (procps-ng 3.3.17), including usage text and quirks. It appears the
builtin delegates to (or exactly clones) procps kill. Reimplementation should reproduce these
strings; they may vary with the host's procps version.

### kill PID (numeric only; job specs NOT supported)
  kill <live-pid>        -> sends SIGTERM, status 0
  kill <pid> <pid2> ...  -> multiple PIDs OK, status 0
  kill 12345 (no such)   -> stderr "kill: (12345): No such process", status 1
  kill %1                -> stderr "kill: failed to parse argument: '%1'", status 1
  kill abc               -> stderr "kill: failed to parse argument: 'abc'", status 1

### signals
  kill -KILL <pid> / kill -9 <pid> / kill -s TERM <pid>   -> all work, status 0
  kill -BOGUS 12345:
      stderr starts "kill: invalid argument B" then the full usage block (below), status 1

### kill (no args) -> usage on STDERR, status 1:
      
      Usage:
       kill [options] <pid> [...]

      Options:
       <pid> [...]            send signal to every <pid> listed
       -<signal>, -s, --signal <signal>
                              specify the <signal> to be sent
       -q, --queue <value>    integer value to be sent with the signal
       -l, --list=[<signal>]  list all signal names, or convert one to a name
       -L, --table            list all signal names in a nice table

       -h, --help     display this help and exit
       -V, --version  output version information and exit

      For more details see kill(1).
  (The block starts with a blank line.)

### kill -l  -> stdout (exit 0):
      HUP INT QUIT ILL TRAP ABRT BUS FPE KILL USR1 SEGV USR2 PIPE ALRM TERM STKFLT
      CHLD CONT STOP TSTP TTIN TTOU URG XCPU XFSZ VTALRM PROF WINCH POLL PWR SYS
### kill -l 15    -> stdout "TERM\n", exit 0
### kill -l BOGUS -> stdout "kill: unknown signal name BOGUS\n", status 0 (!)
### kill -L       -> stdout (exit 0):
       1 HUP      2 INT      3 QUIT     4 ILL      5 TRAP     6 ABRT     7 BUS
       8 FPE      9 KILL    10 USR1    11 SEGV    12 USR2    13 PIPE    14 ALRM
      15 TERM    16 STKFLT  17 CHLD    18 CONT    19 STOP    20 TSTP    21 TTIN
      22 TTOU    23 URG     24 XCPU    25 XFSZ    26 VTALRM  27 PROF    28 WINCH
      29 POLL    30 PWR     31 SYS     
### kill --help    -> usage block (as above) on STDOUT, exit 0
### kill --version -> stdout "kill from procps-ng 3.3.17\n", exit 0

================================================================================
## break / continue
================================================================================

### They take NO arguments. `break 2`, `break foo`, `continue 2` are PARSE ERRORS (exit 255):
  ./executable --norc -c 'for i in 1 2; do break 2; done'
    stderr:
      nsh: parse error:  --> 1:24
        |
      1 | for i in 1 2; do break 2; done
        |                        ^---
        |
        = expected and_or_list_sep or compound_list_sep

### In `for` loops they work correctly (directly, inside if, inside case, via eval):
  for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; break; done; echo after        -> 1, after
  for i in 1 2 3; do continue; echo $i; done; echo after     -> after
  for i in 1 2 3 4; do if test $i -eq 2; then continue; fi; echo $i; done  -> 1 3 4
  for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do if test $i -eq 3; then break; fi; echo $i; done   -> 1 2
  for i in 1 2 3; do case $i in 2) break;; *) echo $i;; esac; done; echo after -> 1, after
  Nested for: break exits only the inner for:
    for i in 1 2 3; do for j in a b c; do echo "$i$j"; break; done; done   -> 1a 2a 3a

### In `while` loops they are BROKEN (this is the surprising part). Model that fits all
  observations: break/continue abort the current command-list evaluation and set a pending
  control-flow signal. `for` consumes it (break=stop, continue=next iteration). `while`
  IGNORES it for loop control — it re-evaluates the condition and keeps looping — and if the
  LAST body execution ended with the signal pending, the signal becomes the while's own result
  and propagates outward.

  Observed cases:
  a) break directly in while body:
       i=0; while test $i -lt 5; do i=$((i+1)); echo $i; break; done; echo after
     -> prints 1 2 3 4 5 (loop NOT broken!), "after" never prints, then PANIC:
        "unexpected Break", exit=101.
  b) continue directly in while body:
       i=0; while test $i -lt 3; do i=$((i+1)); continue; echo $i; done; echo after
     -> prints nothing (body aborted each iteration), then PANIC "unexpected Continue", exit=101.
  c) break inside if inside while:
       ... if test $i -eq 2; then break; echo X; fi; echo "end$i"; done; echo after
     -> at i=2 the rest of the iteration is skipped (acts like continue), loop CONTINUES to
        completion, NO panic, exit=0 (prints iter1,end1,iter2,iter3,end3,after).
  d) continue inside if inside while -> works as a proper continue (1 3 4 after, exit=0).
  e) Pending signal propagates out of while and is consumed by an enclosing for:
       for x in X Y; do i=0; while test $i -lt 2; do i=$((i+1)); echo "$x$i"; break; done;
         echo "innerdone$x"; done; echo after
     -> X1 X2 after   (pending Break aborts for body — "innerdone" skipped — and stops the for)
       same with continue:
     -> X1 X2 Y1 Y2 after   (pending Continue skips rest of for body, for goes on)

### Outside any loop -> PANIC:
  break; echo after     -> stdout empty, exit=101, stderr:
      nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:133:14:
      unexpected Break
      [backtrace, ND]
      nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues
  continue; echo after  -> identical but "unexpected Continue".

### `until` does not exist (parse error), so only for/while matter.

================================================================================
## Panics (shared format)
================================================================================

Triggered by: `return` at top level (also inside source/eval), `break`/`continue` outside a
loop or left pending after a `while` loop.
- stderr first two lines (deterministic):
    nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:133:14:
    unexpected Break            (or: unexpected Continue / unexpected Return)
- then a Rust backtrace with [ND] addresses, then final line:
    nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues
- exit code 101.
- The panic is also appended (ANSI-colored) to ~/.nsh.log.

================================================================================
## CONDENSED RULES
================================================================================

source FILE:
  1. `.` is NOT an alias ("command not found `.'"). No PATH search; relative to CWD.
  2. Runs in current shell; assignments persist; args ignored (not bound to $1...).
  3. Missing file: stderr "nsh: failed open the file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: \"No such file or directory\" }", status 1, continue. Directory: code 21 IsADirectory variant.
  4. No args: "nsh: source: filename argument required", but status 0.
  5. Status = last command's status; `exit N` exits shell with N; `return` panics (101);
     syntax error -> nothing executes, status -1, shell continues.

exec [CMD ARGS...]:
  1. execvp only (no builtins). Success: replaces shell. Failure: "nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory" (status 127) or "nsh: exec: EACCES: Permission denied" (126); shell continues.
  2. No args: no-op, status 0.
  3. Redirections on exec/eval are silently ignored (target file still created/truncated).

eval [ARGS...]:
  1. Args joined with single spaces and re-parsed/executed in current shell.
  2. No args/whitespace: status 0. Status = last command. Parse error inside: message printed,
     status -1, shell continues (overall exit 255 if it was the last command).
  3. exit/return/break/continue inside eval behave as if written inline.

read [-p PROMPT] VAR:
  1. Exactly one VAR. No splitting, no REPLY, IFS ignored, whitespace preserved,
     trailing \n (and \r\n) stripped, backslashes literal.
  2. Status 0 on a line read (incl. unterminated final line); status 1 at EOF (VAR set to "").
  3. -p accepted, prompt never displayed. -r/-s/-n/-t/extra args: clap error on stderr
     ("read: error: Found argument 'X' ..."), status 1, script continues.
  4. Missing VAR: "read: error: The following required arguments were not provided:\n    <VAR>\n\nUSAGE:\n    read [OPTIONS] <VAR>\n\nFor more information try --help", status 1.
  5. --help: help to stderr, exit 1. --version: stdout "read 0.4.2" w/o newline + stderr "read: \n\n", exit 1.
  6. As last pipeline element, runs in the CURRENT shell.

Background / jobs:
  1. Before executing each new command (and before exiting), the shell blocking-waits for all
     bg children and prints "[1] Done: <source text>" to its own stdout for each TRACKED job.
  2. Tracked = external simple commands and pipelines. Builtins, assignments, compound
     commands and subshells run untracked (no notification, no jobs entry) but still block
     the next command.
  3. Job id is always 1; notification always says "Done:" regardless of exit status/signal.
  4. $! = last bg PID ("0" if none).
  5. jobs: prints "[N] Done: ..." lines (always Done non-interactively); any argument ->
     clap error under the wrong name "fg" ("fg: error: Found argument ..."), status 1.
  6. wait: no args -> status 0 always (exit statuses not propagated). "%N" -> "nsh: no such job \`N'";
     anything else -> "nsh: invalid job id \`X'"; status 1.
  7. fg/bg: no jobs -> "nsh: no jobs to run" (status 1); "%N" -> "nsh: no such job \`N'";
     other -> "nsh: invalid job id \`X'".
  8. --help of jobs/fg/bg/wait prints clap help to STDERR, exit 1 (jobs help header is the
     buggy "fg: jobs 0.4.2"; fg's is "nsh: fg: fg 0.4.2").

kill:
  1. Numeric PIDs only: kill [-SIG] PID...; % specs and junk ->
     "kill: failed to parse argument: 'X'" (status 1); dead PID ->
     "kill: (PID): No such process" (status 1); success status 0.
  2. -l (list, exit 0), "-l N" (name), -L (table), --help (stdout, exit 0),
     --version ("kill from procps-ng 3.3.17"). No args or bad signal -> usage on stderr,
     status 1. All text identical to procps-ng 3.3.17 /bin/kill.

break/continue:
  1. No arguments allowed (parse error, exit 255).
  2. Work correctly in `for` (incl. inside if/case/eval); innermost for only.
  3. In `while`: ignored for loop control; they abort the current body command list; if the
     signal is still pending after the while's final iteration, it propagates outward —
     consumed by an enclosing for, or PANIC ("unexpected Break"/"unexpected Continue", 101)
     at top level. break-in-if inside while degrades to a continue-like skip, no panic.
  4. Outside loops: panic main.rs:133, exit 101.

payload.resultSummary:
Spec written to `/workspace/specs/exec_pipes.md` (582 lines). Key findings:

- **`||` is broken**: it behaves exactly like `;` — the RHS always runs (`true || echo x` prints `x`; `echo a || echo b` prints both). `&&` is normal POSIX. `!` is not a reserved word at all (`nsh: command not found \`!'`, exit 1).
- **Background `&` is fully synchronous**: the shell forks, waits, then prints `[1] Done: <raw source of the term>` to *stdout* (job number always 1). One Done per forked pipeline in the term — so `true && true &` prints Done *twice*. Pipelines consisting solely of "in-process" builtins (echo, cd, alias, export, unset, set, eval, source, read, pushd, popd, shift) run inline: no job, no Done, `$!` stays 0, and side effects persist; true/false/printf/pwd/test/[/kill fork. `$!`=0 initially; `wait`/`jobs` are effectively no-ops; `fg`/`bg` → `nsh: no jobs to run` (exit 1).
- **Pipeline segments run in the current shell** — `cd /tmp | cat; pwd` → `/tmp`, `export X=1 | cat` persists. Pipeline status = last command; no pipefail; stderr never piped.
- **Redirections**: `&>`, `&>>`, `<>`, `>|`, redirect-only commands, and leading redirects are parse errors (exit 255, pest-formatted). `<&-`/`2>&-` **panic** (exit 101, ParseIntError); `echo >&9` panics (EBADF). `>>` to a nonexistent file **silently fails** (exit 1, nothing created); all redirect open failures are silent exit 1 with no message. Globs in targets are literal; ordering is POSIX (`>f 2>&1` vs `2>&1 >f` verified).
- **Heredocs**: body lines are *word-processed* — expansions applied, quotes stripped, and whitespace trimmed + collapsed to single spaces (`a  b   c` → `a b c`). No `<<'EOF'`, `<<"EOF"`, `<<<`, `<<-` (the `-` joins the delimiter), no multiple heredocs. Unterminated heredoc = parse error `expected word` at line N+1, exit 255. Empty body yields one empty line.
- **Process substitution**: `<(cmd)` works, yields `/dev/fd/N` starting at 4 per command line, exit status ignored; `>(cmd)` **panics** ("not implemented", exit 101).
- Panics print `nsh: panicked at src/...` + Rust backtrace + a "Something went wrong" footer on stderr, exit 101 (addresses nondeterministic). One rare, non-reproducible race panic (`unexpected Continue`) seen with `sleep & sleep & jobs`.

Spec written to `/workspace/specs/builtins_io.md` (538 lines, exact inputs/outputs/exit codes + condensed rules). Key findings:

- **Background jobs are effectively synchronous in `-c` mode**: before every new command (and before exit), nsh blocking-waits for all bg children and prints `[1] Done: <source text>` to its own stdout. `sleep 1 & echo fast` takes 1s; two `sleep 1 &` take 2s. Job id is always `[1]`, status always `Done:` regardless of exit code/signal. Only external commands/pipelines are tracked — builtins, assignments (`x=5 &` sets x in current shell!), compound commands and subshells run silently but still block.
- **break/continue are broken in `while` loops**: ignored for loop control; a pending signal after the last iteration propagates outward (consumed by an enclosing `for`, or PANIC `unexpected Break/Continue` at `main.rs:133`, exit 101). In `for` they work correctly. `break 2` is a parse error (exit 255); `until` doesn't exist.
- **`return` inside `source`/`eval` panics** the same way (exit 101, backtrace + `~/.nsh.log` entry); `exit N` inside them exits the shell with N.
- **`source`**: `.` is not an alias; no PATH search; args are ignored (not bound to `$1`); missing file gives a Rust `Os { code: 2, ... }` debug-format error, status 1, script continues; syntax error means nothing in the file executes and `$?` becomes `-1`.
- **`exec`/`eval` ignore redirections** (file still created/truncated). exec failure: `nsh: exec: ENOENT: ...` status 127, shell continues.
- **`read` takes exactly ONE var**: no splitting, IFS ignored, whitespace preserved, backslashes literal, `-r/-s/-n/-t` are clap errors; `-p` accepted but the prompt is never displayed even on a pty; EOF → status 1 (unterminated last line → 0).
- **`kill` output is byte-identical to procps-ng 3.3.17 `/bin/kill`** (usage text, `(pid): No such process`, `failed to parse argument`) — likely delegates to it.
- Assorted clap quirks: `--help` for jobs/fg/bg/wait/read goes to **stderr with exit 1**; `jobs` errors use the wrong name `fg:`; `--version` prints without newline plus a stray `read: \n\n` on stderr.

# nsh 0.4.2 — Control Flow, Functions, Subshells, Grouping (observed behavior)

All probes run as `./executable --norc -c 'STRING'` with isolated HOME.
Notation: `exit=N` is the shell's exit code; stdout/stderr shown verbatim.
Line numbers in parse errors are 1-based `LINE:COL`; the `^---` marker points at the column.

NOTE on output formatting quirk (affects many transcripts below): an UNQUOTED
parameter expansion (`$x`, `$?`, `$1`, ...) forms its own word, and any adjacent
literal text becomes separate words, so `echo i=$i` with i=5 prints `i= 5`
(echo joins its args with a space). Quoted `"i=$i"` prints `i=5`. This is an
expansion-stage behavior; it is shown verbatim in transcripts.

## 1. if / then / elif / else / fi

### 1.1 Basic forms
- `if true; then echo yes; fi` → stdout `yes\n`, exit 0.
- `if false; then echo yes; fi` → empty stdout, exit 0 (no condition true, no else ⇒ status 0).
- `if false; then echo yes; else echo no; fi` → `no\n`, exit 0.
- `if true; then false; fi; echo $?` → `1` (status = body's last command).
- Empty body allowed: `if true; then fi` → exit 0, no output.
- Condition may be a pipeline; last command's status decides:
  - `if false | true; then echo T; else echo F; fi` → `T`
  - `if true | false; then echo T; else echo F; fi` → `F`
- `&&` / `||` work in conditions: `if true && false; then echo T; else echo F; fi` → `F`.
- `!` is NOT a keyword: `! true; echo $?` → stderr `nsh: command not found \`!'\n`, prints `1`.
  `if ! false; then echo y; fi` → same stderr, no `y` (status 1 ⇒ else branch).
- Assignment-only condition works and persists: `if x=1; then echo then-ran; fi; echo x=$x` → `then-ran\nx= 1`.
- Condition may itself be a compound `if`: `while if true; then false; fi; do echo b; done; echo end` → `end`.

### 1.2 **elif BUG (important)**
When the initial `if` condition is FALSE and ANY `elif` condition evaluates true,
nsh executes the **if's `then` body** (not the matching elif's body), then stops.
Elif conditions are evaluated in order until the first true one; later elif
conditions are not evaluated. If no elif is true, the else body runs (or nothing).

- `if false; then echo a; elif true; then echo b; else echo c; fi` → `a` (POSIX would print `b`)
- `if false; then echo a; elif true; then echo b; fi` → `a`
- `if false; then echo a; elif false; then echo b; else echo c; fi` → `c` (no true elif ⇒ else)
- `if false; then echo a; elif false; then echo b; elif false; then echo c; elif true; then echo d; else echo e; fi` → `a`
- `if true; then echo a; elif true; then echo b; else echo c; fi` → `a` (if-cond true: normal; elif conds NOT evaluated)

cat > /workspace/specs/runtime.md <<'SPEC_EOF'
# nsh 0.4.2 — Runtime errors, exit statuses, signals, misc runtime (observed behavior)

All probes run as `./executable --norc -c 'STRING'` with isolated HOME (`HOME=/tmp/nshprobe`),
unless stated otherwise. `exit=N` = the nsh process exit code; `$?` = status observed inside.
stdout/stderr shown verbatim (line-end `$` markers from `sed -n l` removed here unless ambiguous).

CROSS-CUTTING QUIRK (also documented in expansion.md): an UNQUOTED parameter expansion
forms its own word, detached from adjacent literal text. `echo q=$?` with `$?`=1 prints
`q= 1` (three words: `q=`, `1` → echo joins with a space). Quoted `"q=$?"` prints `q=1`.
Transcripts below show this verbatim.

NONDETERMINISM: panic backtraces contain ASLR addresses (`0x...`) that vary per run, and the
stack-overflow message contains a PID. File paths, message text, and exit codes are stable.

================================================================================
## 1. Command not found / exec failures (status is 1, NOT 127)
================================================================================

### 1.1 Command not found (bare name, PATH search)
- `-c 'nonexistent_xyz'` → stderr `nsh: command not found \`nonexistent_xyz'\n`, empty stdout, exit=1.
- `-c 'nonexistent_xyz; echo "q=$?"'` → stderr same message, stdout `q=1`, exit=0.
  ⇒ `$?` after command-not-found is **1** (not 127).
- Message quotes name with backtick + apostrophe: `` `NAME' ``. Only the command word is shown, never args.
- Empty command name: `-c '""; echo "q=$?"'` → stderr ``nsh: command not found `'` `` + `q=1`.
- Name with space: `-c '"non existent"'` → stderr ``nsh: command not found `non existent'``.
- PATH search skips non-executable files silently: file `pathed` (mode 644) in PATH dir,
  `export PATH=/tmp/rtfx; pathed` → `nsh: command not found \`pathed'`, status 1.
  (Same message whether the file is absent or present-but-not-executable.)

### 1.2 Name contains a slash (direct exec, no PATH search)
- Nonexistent: `-c '/tmp/nshfx/no_such_file_xyz'` →
  stderr `nsh: Failed to exec "/tmp/nshfx/no_such_file_xyz" (ENOENT: No such file or directory)\n`, status 1.
  Same for relative: `-c './no_such_file_xyz'` → `nsh: Failed to exec "./no_such_file_xyz" (ENOENT: No such file or directory)`.
- Exists, not executable (mode 644): `-c '/tmp/nshfx/noexec.sh'` →
  stderr `nsh: Failed to exec "/tmp/nshfx/noexec.sh" (EACCESS). chmod(1) may help.\n`, status 1.
  (Note the literal token `EACCESS` — double-S — and the `chmod(1) may help.` suffix.)
- Is a directory: `-c '/tmp/nshfx/somedir'` → same EACCESS message:
  `nsh: Failed to exec "/tmp/nshfx/somedir" (EACCESS). chmod(1) may help.`, status 1.
  (Directory via a MISSING path component still gives ENOENT: `./somedir` before mkdir →
  `nsh: Failed to exec "./somedir" (ENOENT: No such file or directory)`.)
- Executable file without shebang (ENOEXEC) — nsh does NOT fall back to running it as a script:
  file mode 755 containing `echo frompathx` →
  `nsh: Failed to exec "/tmp/rtfx/pathedx" (ENOEXEC: Exec format error)`, status 1.
- In all slash cases `$?` = 1.

### 1.3 PATH lookup semantics (quirks)
- PATH is read from the EXPORTED environment only. A plain assignment statement does NOT
  affect lookup: `PATH=/tmp/rtfx; pathedx` → `command not found \`pathedx'` (file exists, mode 755!).
  `export PATH=/tmp/rtfx; pathedx` → attempts exec (ENOEXEC message, see 1.2).
- Assignment PREFIX does not affect lookup either: `PATH=/tmp/rtfx pathedx` → `command not found \`pathedx'`.
- `unset PATH; ls` WORKS — with PATH unset, nsh falls back to a built-in default PATH.
  `env -i ./executable --norc -c 'echo "PATH=$PATH"; ls'` → prints
  `PATH=/sbin:/usr/sbin:/usr/local/sbin:/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin` and `ls` succeeds (exit 0).
  So the default PATH string is exactly: `/sbin:/usr/sbin:/usr/local/sbin:/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin`.
- `PATH=` (empty value as a statement) is a PARSE ERROR: `-c 'PATH=; ls'` →
  ```
  nsh: parse error:  --> 1:6
    |
  1 | PATH=; ls
    |      ^---
    |
    = expected literal_span, tilde_span, any_string_span, any_char_span, command_span, proc_subst_direction, backtick_span, expr_span, param_ex_span, param_span, double_quoted_span, single_quoted_span, or initializer
  ```
  exit=255. Same for `FOO=` alone (error at col 5). An empty value is only legal...
  actually see next item — even weirder:
- EMPTY-VALUE PREFIX ASSIGNMENT SWALLOWS THE NEXT WORD: `-c 'FOO= echo; echo "[$FOO]"'`
  → stdout `[echo]`, exit 0. No command was executed; `FOO` got the value `echo`.
  `-c 'FOO= echo "[$FOO]"; echo "q=$?"'` → stderr ``nsh: command not found `[]' ``,
  stdout `q=1` (FOO=echo consumed `echo`; the remaining word `[$FOO]` expanded to `[]`
  and was executed as the command name).

### 1.4 exec builtin failures
- `-c 'exec /nonexistent_xyz; echo "after=$?"'` → stderr `nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory\n`,
  stdout `after=127`, exit 0. ⇒ failed exec sets `$?`=127 and the shell CONTINUES (does not exit).
- `-c 'exec /tmp; echo "after=$?"'` → stderr `nsh: exec: EACCES: Permission denied\n`, stdout `after=126`.
  (Here the errno names are `ENOENT`/`EACCES`, colon-separated — different format from §1.2.)

================================================================================
## 2. Script-file argument (./executable --norc FILE)
================================================================================
- File without exec bit (mode 644) RUNS FINE as a script (read + interpreted). exit = last command's status.
- File ends with `false` → exit 1. Ends with command-not-found → exit 1. `exit 7` → exit 7.
- Missing script file → PANIC (see §5), exit 101:
  first lines: `nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:114:34:` then
  `failed to open the file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }`
- Script path is a directory → PANIC, exit 101:
  `nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:114:34:` then
  `failed to open the file: Os { code: 21, kind: IsADirectory, message: "Is a directory" }`
- Script containing non-UTF-8 bytes → PANIC, exit 101:
  `nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:114:34:` then
  `failed to open the file: Error { kind: InvalidData, message: "stream did not contain valid UTF-8" }`

================================================================================
## 3. stdin (no -c, no script arg)
================================================================================
- `printf 'echo hi\nfalse\n' | ./executable --norc` →
  stderr `nsh: warning: stdout is not a tty\n`, NO other output, exit 0. THE SCRIPT IS NOT EXECUTED.
  Same when stdin is a redirected file or closed (`<&-`): warning on stderr, exit 0, nothing runs.
  (The warning text says "stdout" even though the trigger is the non-interactive session.)
- stdin given AND `-c` given → `-c` runs normally, stdin ignored, no warning.

================================================================================
## 4. Exit-status model
================================================================================
- Overall `-c` / script exit code = status of last executed command (e.g. ends with `false` → 1;
  command-not-found → 1). Initial `$?` is 0 (`-c 'echo "s=$?"'` → `s=0`).
- Parse error ANYWHERE in the string → NOTHING executes (whole string parsed first),
  exit 255. `-c 'echo hi; $('` → no `hi`; stderr:
  ```
  nsh: parse error:  --> 1:12
    |
  1 | echo hi; $(
    |            ^---
    |
    = expected command or compound_list_sep
  ```
  exit=255.
- `-c ''`, `-c '# just a comment'`, whitespace-only → silent, exit 0.
- `exit N`: exit code = N mod 256. `exit 3` → 3; `exit 300` → 44; `exit 256` → 0; `exit 257` → 1;
  `exit -1` → 255; `exit -2` → 254.
- `exit` with NO argument exits **0**, IGNORING `$?`: `-c 'false; exit'` → exit 0 (POSIX would be 1).
- `exit` with non-numeric argument exits **1**, silently (no error message):
  `exit abc` → 1; `exit 1abc` → 1; `exit 12abc` → 1; `exit 1.5` → 1.
- External command terminated by a signal: `$?` is **-1** (printed literally as `-1`), no message:
  `-c 'sh -c "kill -TERM $$"; echo "q=$?"'` → stdout `q=-1`, exit 0.
  Same for SIGKILL, SIGSEGV. If it is the LAST command, the overall exit code is **255**
  (i.e. -1 truncated to u8): `-c 'sh -c "kill -TERM $$"'` → exit 255, no output.
  Contrast: nsh itself dying from a signal (next section) is reported by the PARENT as 128+N.

================================================================================
## 5. Panics (Rust panic handler) — exit code 101
================================================================================
Deterministic shape of stderr for a panic:
```
nsh: panicked at src/<file>:<line>:<col>:
<panic message>
nsh:    0:     0x<addr> - backtrace::backtrace::libunwind::trace::h...
<... full symbolized backtrace, ~15-25 frames, includes /workspace/src/*.rs paths
     and /rustc/... and /usr/local/cargo/registry/... paths; addresses vary per run ...>

nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues
```
- Blank line between last backtrace frame and the `Something went wrong` line.
- Process exit code is **101**. Nothing of the pending script executes after a panic.
- The panic is also appended to `~/.nsh.log` with ANSI colors, format:
  `\x1b[1m[\x1b[31mERROR\x1b[0m\t]\x1b[0m \x1b[36msrc/main.rs\x1b[0m: <message>` (one ERROR entry per line of message/backtrace).

Observed panic triggers (file:line:col + exact message):
| Trigger | Location | Message |
|---|---|---|
| `return` at top level (also `return 5`) | src/main.rs:133:14 | `unexpected Return` |
| `break` at top level | src/main.rs:133:14 | `unexpected Break` |
| `continue` at top level | src/main.rs:133:14 | `unexpected Continue` |
| arithmetic division by zero, `echo $((1/0))` | src/eval.rs:38:47 | `attempt to divide by zero` |
| `**` in arithmetic, `echo $((2**8))` (parsed as `$(` subst of `(2**8)`, glob `**` fails) | src/pattern.rs:73:41 | `failed to glob: PatternError { pos: 0, msg: "recursive wildcards must form a single path component" }` |
| builtin echo write error, `echo x > /dev/full` | src/utils.rs:51:47 | `failed to write: ENOSPC` |
| script arg missing/dir/non-UTF8 | src/main.rs:114:34 | `failed to open the file: ...` (see §2) |
| non-UTF-8 bytes inside the `-c` ARGV itself | .../clap-2.34.0/src/args/arg_matches.rs:121:40 | `unexpected invalid UTF-8 code point` |

Note: `$((1/0))` panic fires during word expansion — earlier words on the same line are lost
(no output), and NOTHING after it runs. For `echo $((2*3)) $((7-10)) $((2**8))` the stdout
`6 -3 ` (with trailing space) WAS produced before the panic because `2**8` is evaluated in a
command-substitution subshell whose partial output had already been written.

================================================================================
## 6. Arithmetic edge cases
================================================================================
- `/` by zero → panic, exit 101 (see §5).
- `%` is NOT in the arithmetic grammar: `$((4%3))` is parsed as `$(` command substitution of
  the subshell command `(4%3)` → the inner subshell tries to run command `4%3` →
  stderr ``nsh: command not found `4%3' ``; the substitution yields empty; `echo $((4%3)); echo "q=$?"`
  → stdout empty line + `q=0`, exit 0. (The failure is hidden inside the substitution.)
- `**` → glob panic (see §5). `+ - * /` and parentheses work: `$(((1+2)*3))` → `9`,
  `$((7-10))` → `-3`.

================================================================================
## 7. Stack depth / recursion
================================================================================
- Infinite function recursion `f(){ f; }; f` → process dies from stack overflow:
  stderr exactly (PID varies):
  ```

  thread 'main' (<PID>) has overflowed its stack
  fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting
  ```
  (leading blank line; then the shell aborts with SIGABRT — parent sees exit 134).
- Parser/evaluator recursion limits on INPUT SIZE: a script of N `echo x` lines:
  N=1000 → ok; N=5000 → ok (~seconds); N=10000 → >30s, partial output (quadratic-ish slowdown);
  N=50000 → same stack-overflow abort (134) with zero output.
- Single very long lines are fine: 1 MB and 10 MB one-line `echo aaaa...` scripts run, exit 0,
  output length 1000001 / 10000001. (A 10 MB `-c` ARGUMENT is impossible to test: execve
  MAX_ARG_STRLEN kills it before nsh runs — bash itself reports exit 126.)

================================================================================
## 8. Background jobs, `wait`, `jobs`, `$!` (non-interactive -c mode)
================================================================================
Mechanism appears to be: bg job spawns an intermediate child that exits IMMEDIATELY while the
real command keeps running (nsh acts as subreaper and can still wait for it). Observable rules:

- Starting ANY background job prints, to STDOUT, immediately (before the next command's output):
  `[1] Done: <command line as typed>\n` — e.g. `/bin/sleep 5 & echo A` →
  ```
  [1] Done: /bin/sleep 5
  A
  ```
  The `[1] Done` is printed even though the command is still running. Job id is `1` again for
  every new job (two sequential `&` jobs both print `[1] Done: ...`).
- `jobs` prints NOTHING right after starting a bg job (job already considered Done/removed).
- `$!` is set to the intermediate child's PID, which is already dead when used:
  - `ps -p $!` → no such process; `ls -d /proc/$!` → cannot access;
  - `/bin/kill -TERM $!` → `kill: (<pid>): No such process` (from util-linux kill), status 1.
  - `$!` before any bg job expands to `0`: `echo "[$!]"` → `[0]`.
- `wait` (no args): BLOCKS until the real background command finishes (verified by timing:
  `sleep 3 & wait` takes ~3.0s), then returns 0 — even if the command exited non-zero
  (`sh -c 'exit 3' & wait` → `$?`=0).
- `wait %1` right after starting: also blocks until the command finishes, THEN prints
  stderr ``nsh: no such job `1' `` and returns 1.
- `wait %7` (never existed): stderr ``nsh: no such job `7' ``, status 1 (immediate).
- `wait <numeric pid>`: stderr ``nsh: invalid job id `<pid>' ``, status 1 (immediate).
- Shell exit WAITS for orphaned background commands: `-c '/bin/sleep 5 & echo started'` takes
  ~5.0s total, exit 0. `-c '/bin/sleep 0.1 &'` → prints `[1] Done: /bin/sleep 0.1`, exit 0.
- `fg` / `bg` with no jobs: stderr `nsh: no jobs to run\n`, status 1 (both).

================================================================================
## 9. kill is NOT a builtin
================================================================================
- `export PATH=/nonexistent_dir; kill -l` → ``nsh: command not found `kill' ``.
  All `kill` invocations resolve to external `/bin/kill` (util-linux):
  - `kill` (no args) → util-linux usage text on stderr (starts with blank line then `Usage:`...), status 1.
  - `kill -NOSUCH %1` → stderr `kill: invalid argument N\n` + same usage text, status 1.
  - `kill 1` → sends SIGTERM to PID 1, status 0 (we run as root).
  - `kill %1` / `kill -TERM %1` → util-linux rejects `%1`; the bg job keeps running.
- `kill -TERM $$` (as a -c command) kills the nsh process itself → parent observes exit 143,
  nsh prints NOTHING itself. Any `Terminated`/`Killed` text seen in a terminal comes from the
  PARENT shell's job notification, not from nsh. Same for `(kill -INT $$)` → 130,
  `(kill -KILL $$)` → 137: `$$` in a subshell is the top shell's PID, so these kill the whole nsh.

================================================================================
## 10. Signals delivered TO the nsh process (-c mode)
================================================================================
- SIGINT while a foreground child runs: nsh dies immediately with signal; parent sees exit 130.
  No message, no cleanup output; the rest of the -c string never runs. Same when sent to the
  whole process group.
- SIGTERM → parent sees 143. No output.
- nsh NEVER prints bash-style `Terminated`/`Segmentation fault` notifications for children
  killed by signals (neither for external commands nor subshells); the only trace is `$?`=-1
  (§4) or the parent's own report.

================================================================================
## 11. Redirection runtime errors
================================================================================
- Output redirect into nonexistent directory: `echo x > /nonexistent_dir_xyz/f` →
  SILENT (no stderr), `$?`=1, nothing on stdout.
- Output redirect onto a directory: `echo x > /tmp` → SILENT, `$?`=1.
- Input redirect from missing file: `cat < /missing` → SILENT, `$?`=1.
- Ordering/partial application: `echo ran > /tmp/rtfx/ran.txt < /nonexistent_xyz` →
  ran.txt IS created/truncated (0 bytes), then the failing `<` aborts the command:
  `$?`=1, silent, echo never runs (file stays empty).
- Files created by `>` get mode 0666 & ~umask: 0644 with umask 022, 0600 with umask 077.
- Write errors on the TARGET are not silent: builtin echo to a full device PANICS
  (`echo x > /dev/full` → `nsh: panicked at src/utils.rs:51:47:` / `failed to write: ENOSPC`, exit 101).
  builtin printf to /dev/full instead prints `printf: write error: No space left on device`
  (coreutils-style wording) on stderr, `$?`=1.
- SIGPIPE: `echo x | true` → fine, `$?`=0. But `yes | head -1` HANGS forever (prints one `y`,
  then neither side dies — nsh leaves SIGPIPE ignored/inherited or fds open; observed 3/3 runs).
  A pipeline like `ps -eo pid,comm | grep -w sleep` works normally otherwise.

================================================================================
## 12. Tilde expansion runtime behavior
================================================================================
- `echo ~` → $HOME (`/tmp/nshprobe` in probes). No warning.
- `echo ~root` or `~nosuchuserxyz` → stderr `nsh: warning: ~user is not yet supported\n`
  and the word expands to $HOME ANYWAY (regardless of whether the user exists). Status 0.
- `echo ~+ ~-` → BOTH treated as ~user forms: two warnings, both expand to $HOME.
- HOME unset: `~` falls back to the passwd database (getpwuid): `env -u HOME ... -c 'echo ~'`
  → `/root`; bare `cd` goes there too. Same under `env -i`.

================================================================================
## 13. cd runtime errors
================================================================================
- `cd /nonexistent_xyz` → stderr `nsh: cd: No such file or directory (os error 2): \`/nonexistent_xyz'\n`,
  `$?`=1, cwd unchanged.
- `cd /etc/hostname` (a file) → stderr `nsh: cd: Not a directory (os error 20): \`/etc/hostname'\n`, `$?`=1.
  (Rust std::io::Error Display format: `<message> (os error <n>)`.)

================================================================================
## 14. Misc
================================================================================
- `$RANDOM` is NOT supported: expands to empty. `echo $RANDOM; echo $RANDOM` → two empty lines;
  `echo "$RANDOM $RANDOM $RANDOM"` → `  ` (two spaces).
- `source /missing` → stderr `nsh: failed open the file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }\n`
  (note literal `failed open` — no "to"), `$?`=1, shell continues.
- `.` is NOT source: `. /missing` → ``nsh: command not found `.' ``, `$?`=1.
- `builtin`, `type`, `command` etc. are not builtins (per brief); missing builtins behave as
  ordinary command-not-found.
- NUL bytes in a script file pass THROUGH as regular characters: script `echo a\0echo b`
  (literal NUL) prints the bytes `a\x00echo b\n` (builtin echo emits the NUL). No error.
- Non-UTF-8 bytes: cannot appear in `-c` argv (clap panic §5) or in script files (panic §2);
  bytes produced by EXTERNAL commands pass through transparently.
- nsh creates `~/.nsh_history` (empty) and `~/.nsh.log` in HOME even with `--norc`.
- Default file perms, default PATH, `$?`=−1-for-signals, exit-code-mod-256: see §§4, 11, 1.3.

================================================================================
## 15. Condensed RULES (for reimplementation)
================================================================================
1. Command not found → stderr ``nsh: command not found `<word>' ``, status 1 (never 127).
2. Slash-path exec failure → `nsh: Failed to exec "<path>" (<ERR>). chmod(1) may help.` for
   EACCES/EISDIR (literal `EACCESS`), `nsh: Failed to exec "<path>" (ENOENT: No such file or directory)`,
   `nsh: Failed to exec "<path>" (ENOEXEC: Exec format error)`; status 1; no script fallback.
3. PATH lookup uses exported PATH only; unset PATH ⇒ default
   `/sbin:/usr/sbin:/usr/local/sbin:/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin`; non-executable PATH members
   are skipped silently (still "command not found").
4. Exit status of shell = last command status; parse error anywhere ⇒ nothing runs, exit 255.
5. `exit` no-arg ⇒ 0; non-numeric arg ⇒ 1 (silent); numeric ⇒ mod 256.
6. Signal-killed child ⇒ `$?` = −1 (no message); as last command ⇒ shell exit 255.
7. Any internal panic ⇒ stderr `nsh: panicked at <loc>:` + message + symbolized backtrace +
   blank line + `nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues`,
   exit 101; also logged ANSI-colored to ~/.nsh.log.
8. `return`/`break`/`continue` at top level ⇒ panic `unexpected Return|Break|Continue` (main.rs:133:14).
9. Division by zero ⇒ panic `attempt to divide by zero` (eval.rs:38:47), exit 101.
10. Deep recursion / huge scripts ⇒ `\nthread 'main' (<pid>) has overflowed its stack\nfatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting\n`, SIGABRT (parent sees 134).
11. Background job ⇒ immediate stdout line `[1] Done: <cmd>`; `$!` = short-lived intermediate pid
    (0 if none yet); `jobs` empty; `wait` blocks for the real command, returns 0;
    `wait %N` blocks then ``nsh: no such job `N' `` status 1; numeric arg ⇒
    ``nsh: invalid job id `<arg>' `` status 1; shell waits for bg jobs before exiting.
12. No `kill` builtin (external util-linux kill used, incl. its usage/error text and `%job` rejection).
13. Signal to nsh itself: dies silently (128+N as seen by parent). No child-death notifications ever.
14. Redirect open failures: silent, status 1; earlier redirects already applied (file created).
    New files: 0666 & ~umask. Write failure in builtin echo ⇒ panic ENOSPC; in builtin printf ⇒
    `printf: write error: No space left on device`, status 1.
15. `~user`/`~+`/`~-` ⇒ stderr warning `nsh: warning: ~user is not yet supported`, expand to $HOME;
    plain `~` silent; HOME unset ⇒ passwd lookup.
16. cd failure ⇒ `nsh: cd: <io error Display>: \`<path>'`, status 1.
17. exec builtin failure ⇒ `nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory` (127) /
    `nsh: exec: EACCES: Permission denied` (126); shell continues.
18. Non-tty session without -c/script ⇒ `nsh: warning: stdout is not a tty` on stderr, exit 0, runs nothing.
19. `-c ''`/comments-only ⇒ exit 0, silent. Script-file read failures panic (main.rs:114:34), exit 101.
20. $RANDOM unsupported (empty). `.` not source. `source` failure: `nsh: failed open the file: Os { ... }`, status 1.
21. Unquoted `$x` always splits into separate word(s), detaching adjacent literals (`echo q=$?` → `q= 1`).
22. `%` and `**` are not arithmetic operators: `$((a%b))` runs `a%b` as a command inside `$(...)`
    (hidden failure, outer status unaffected); `$((a**b))` panics via the glob path.
SPEC_EOF
wc -l /workspace/specs/runtime.md; echo "written, exit=$?"
